entries.title: White Sox hitting director Ryan Fuller talks offensive improvement, and the development that remains
entries.summary: <p>In his second season, White Sox hitting director Ryan Fuller expected the offense to be improved.</p><p>He would not have promised the highest-scoring unit (4.74 runs per game entering Wednesday) in the American League, even when hitting coach Derek Shomon was foretelling top-10 production in spring</p><p>“At the time, it was man, we’ve got a ton of talent, but it's going to be a lot of things coming together the right way to achieve that,” Fuller told the Sun-Times.</p><p>Fuller refers to Shomon, assistant hitting coach Joel McKeithan and major league assistant Tony Medina as the “boots on the ground,” rallying Sox hitters through day-to-day challenges, and reinforcing larger initiatives. Broadly, the White Sox are scoring more this year because they are hitting for more power than anticipated.</p><p>Colson Montgomery, Munetaka Murakami and Miguel Vargas all posting 30-homer campaigns lead an offense that is sixth in MLB in home runs, and looks primed to clear the 200-homer threshold for the first time since 2012. The raw pop of Murakami and Montgomery was previously established. For others, it had to be developed.</p><p>“Last year, 30th in bat speed; we don't want to be last in any meaningful category, so obviously that was a focus,” Fuller told the Sun-Times. “It's the fifth highest year-over-year bat speed increase in the big leagues, so a lot to be proud of.”</p><p>With Chase Meidroth, Sam Antonacci, and Vargas being the largest beneficiary, Fuller says the increased capacity for hard contact is three-pronged. Vargas is also the best example of a player that was challenged to add strength and explosiveness in their offseason training, and Fuller credited the coaching staff and biomechanists for cleaning out swing inefficiencies. But the most prominent addition is a regimen of weighted bat training, using branded equipment from renowned private training facility Driveline, a practice mirrored throughout their minor league system.</p><p>Though developing power provided the biggest White Sox’ offensive gains, Fuller extols the importance of contact-oriented hitters like Meidroth and Antonacci for balancing out the lineup on nights where home runs don’t come. Unlike some analysts, Fuller values a pesky two-strike approach and swing, after hunting for damage early in the count. And the Sox wouldn’t hit at all if they weren’t utilizing simulated at-bats off their Trajekt machine to chase out of the zone less than any point of their recorded history.</p><p>Some of the White Sox offensive identity is simply personnel. They have the fourth-lowest contact rate in the league because their roster is full of loose movers, long levers and uphill swing paths. Their runs come in huge chunks, as do the whiffs and inconsistency, especially with the roster’s youth.</p><p>“It's not like we're the Dodgers, where guys have been in the league for five-plus years, and you really understand their profiles,” Fuller said. “The adjustments they're going to make, understanding how pitchers are attacking them better. We believe that those are going to get to a spot where they're going to be stable.”</p><p>That extends to the White Sox’ currently most embattled hitter and for most of the year, their biggest revelation in Murakami. On Wednesday, Murakami’s brutal slump took another bleak turn, as his streak of consecutive plate appearances with a strikeout reached eight until he was hit by a pitch in the sixth.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/09/03/white-sox-keeping-luis-castillo-in-rotation-and-munetaka-murakami-high-in-batting-order-amid-struggles-will-venable-astros-road-trip-zach-bove-al-central-division-playoffs" target="_blank" ><u>Murakami said in Houston</u></a> that he felt his swing path had become too uphill, requiring his timing and pitch selection to be letter-perfect to make contact. Fuller echoed those sentiments, saying the first baseman’s batting cage work is focused on returning to the baselines of his All-Star caliber start. That he and Sox hitters are ahead of schedule, never assured that there wasn’t more work to do.</p><p>“If it were any other rookie, we would be saying it’s part of the learning experience,” Fuller said. “For these guys to be as successful as they have been in their early part of their careers, learning lessons, making adjustments, and then coming back productive, that's the goal.”</p>

entries.title: Des Plaines police officer fatally shoots man while responding to domestic disturbance
entries.summary: <p>A man died after a Des Plaines police officer shot him during a response to a domestic dispute, according to police.</p><p>Officers were responding to a “domestic disturbance” at a home in the 2000 block of Touhy Avenue at 2:32 p.m. when an officer shot Ayham Babidi, 21, during the encounter, police said. No other details about the shooting were released.</p><p>Babidi was taken to a local hospital where he later died, according to police. The Des Plaines Major Case Assistance Team is investigating.</p>

entries.title: Kevin Gausman gives up three homers, and Cubs’ starting staff stays inconsistent heading toward October
entries.summary: <p>MILWAUKEE – Are <b>Jed Hoyer</b>’s worst fears coming true?</p><p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a>’ team president <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/09/01/cubs-home-runs-record-jed-hoyer-front-office-pitching-starting-rotation-playoffs-postseason-shota-imanaga-matthew-boyd" >cited an inconsistent pitching staff as a concern</a> during his most recent meeting with the media, and a week later, he hasn’t been given any reason to think those issues have been ironed out.</p><p>“The position-playing group, we’re the No. 1 offense, No. 1 defense right now. That’s wonderful. Obviously, that’s the backbone of our team,” Hoyer said last week. “There’s no question of what our strength is. [But] we do need to get consistent starting pitching, throw strikes consistently and hopefully let the position players do the work.”</p><p>While a stumbling bullpen is generating the most fan complaints, it was starter <b>Kevin Gausman</b> – imported by Hoyer’s front office at the trade deadline to be a top-of-the-rotation arm – who was knocked around by the Brewers on Wednesday, crushed for three homers and seven runs in his briefest outing as a Cub to date.</p><p>A night after lefty <b>David Peterson</b> didn’t make it out of the fifth inning, Gausman lasted just four innings, his third Cubs start not to make it to a 15th out.</p><p>Gausman has gone back and forth between looking capable of starting (and dominating) Game 1 of a playoff series and getting hit around.</p><p>In other words, he’s been inconsistent, adding fuel to Hoyer’s nightmares that a hit-or-miss pitching staff could help sink the Cubs in the playoffs.</p><p>Though lefty <b>Shota Imanaga</b> has received season-long attention for surrendering long balls – he entered Wednesday still leading the majors with 33 home runs given up – Gausman has been taken deep plenty since coming to the Cubs in a trade at the beginning of last month, now with nine homers on his tab in seven starts.</p><p>Hoyer spent big, in terms of prospects, at the deadline to net Gausman and fellow right-hander <b>Clay Holmes</b>, whose worst outing as a Cub came Sunday, when he allowed a career-worst eight runs and didn’t make it out of the fifth inning.</p><p>Gausman has now had three starts in a Cubs uniform allowing at least five runs, the sort of thing that can tank a playoff game – and a season, along with it.</p><p>That’s not what Hoyer envisioned, obviously, and though Gausman and Holmes – who pitched in the two most recent World Series, respectively – have the experience and ability to straighten things out, that inconsistency is evidently worth fretting about for the guy running the show.</p><p>On top of it all, this wasn’t some random team on the other end of a bad outing. These Brewers are the team that have owned the NL Central, eliminated the Cubs from the playoffs last year and figure to stand in their way again this October.</p><p>If the Cubs are going to clear the Brewers-shaped hurdle in front of them, they need what Hoyer said they need: more consistency from their arms.</p><p><b>Helping Happ heal</b></p><p>Left fielder <b>Ian Happ</b> was in the Cubs’ lineup Wednesday a day after fouling a pitch off his foot the night before, serving as the DH instead of playing the outfield.</p><p>“It’s a little sore today,” manager <b>Craig Counsell</b> said. “He didn’t feel great cutting and things like that, so we’ll try to minimize the impact and the exposure to it with the DH.”</p><p><b>Surgery for Maton</b></p><p>Counsell relayed that righty reliever <b>Phil Maton</b> will have surgery on his ailing knee later this week.</p><p>The Cubs inked Maton to a two-year free-agent deal in the offseason, but bedeviled by the knee injury throughout the summer, he was ineffective when on the mound, the owner of a 6.18 ERA.</p>

entries.title: Police investigating death of woman pulled from Little Calumet River
entries.summary: <p>Chicago police are investigating after a woman was pulled from the Little Calumet River in West Pullman Wednesday morning and later died, according to the department.</p><p>Ralphealle Howard, 26, was pulled out of the water in the 13000 block of South Indiana Avenue at 10:48 a.m., police said. She was taken to Roseland Hospital, where she later died.</p><p>Her death is under investigation.</p>

entries.title: Lincoln-Way East students walk out to denounce racism their classmates directed at Homewood-Flossmoor peers
entries.summary: <p>Dozens of students walked out of Lincoln-Way East High School in south suburban Frankfort Wednesday morning in support of students at nearby Homewood-Flossmoor High School. </p><p>The Lincoln-Way East students were protesting after two incidents of racial harassment involving their school and H-F.</p><p>The first occurred Friday when Lincoln-Way East students were caught on video racially taunting H-F students at a football game in Flossmoor by mimicking monkeys.</p><p>Then on Saturday, H-F officials said a coach and members of Lincoln-Way East’s girls cross country team racially taunted the H-F team at a meet in west suburban Western Springs.</p><p>The events prompted Lincoln-Way East students to denounce what transpired and support their peers impacted by the acts.</p><p>The mood was somber and the halls were nearly empty at Lincoln-Way East ahead of the demonstration. But the students who remained said they were determined to make their voices heard.</p><p>“We want to let people know that Lincoln-Way East is not just a predominantly white school that's full of racist people,” said 14-year-old Teniola Omokaye. “There's a big demographic of Black people that go here and we actually stand for something.”</p><p>Student organizers <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/high-school-football/2026/09/08/lincoln-way-east-racial-incident-homewood-flossmoor" >planned the walkout</a> to stand with Homewood-Flossmoor High School and send a message that the behavior does not represent the broader Lincoln-Way East student body.</p><p>Students, followed by faculty and staff, streamed out of the school chanting “Black lives matter” and “No place for racism,” as parents and community members cheered them on from across the street.</p><p></p><p></p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/high-school-sports/2026/09/08/lincoln-way-east-racist-incident-homewood-flossmoor" >Second racist Lincoln-Way East incident alleged by Homewood-Flossmoor</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Lincoln-Way East acknowledged what happened at Friday’s football game and apologized. The Lincoln-Way School District, however, denied the allegations involving the girls cross-country team in a statement issued Tuesday afternoon.</p><p>In an earlier statement, H-F Supt. Jennifer Norrell and Principal Clinton Alexander said the school would consider legal options "to protect against this in the future."</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div East said they felt “embarrassed,” but not surprised, to learn that their classmates had been caught making the alleged comments.</p><p>Omokaye said she hadn’t experienced racism at school herself, but she knew other students had.</p><p>“It's unfortunate that my peers have been targeted, and some of them even fear walking in the hallways,” said the first-year student.</p><p>Latoya, who asked that her last name not be published to protect her son, said he has been the target of racist comments from other students at the school.</p><p>She said the 16-year-old was targeted by upperclass students when he was a first-year student. They called him the “N-word” and threw food at him, she said. When Latoya alerted school officials, she said, they only moved her son’s seat away from the students accused of harassing him.</p><p>“The students making these comments are taught the behavior at home, but it’s the school’s responsibility to punish them when they are threatening the safety and learning of others,” Latoya, 50, said.</p><p>Officials at Lincoln-Way East and Homewood-Flossmoor could not immediately be reached for comment.</p>

entries.title: 16-year-old boy fatally shot in South Loop
entries.summary: <p>A teen was fatally shot in South Loop Wednesday night, according to Chicago police.</p><p>The 16-year-old boy was found with a gunshot wound to the neck in the 1100 block of South Michigan Avenue at 9:05 p.m., police said.</p><p>He was taken to Northwestern Hospital in serious condition and later died.</p><p>No one is in custody.</p>

entries.title: Lionel Messi and Robert Lewandowski help Fire draw franchise-record crowd in 1-1 tie with Inter Miami
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/fire" >Fire</a> president of business operations Dave Baldwin was busy in the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/fire/2026/09/08/soccer-spotlight-to-be-on-chicago-when-robert-lewandowski-and-the-fire-host-lionel-messis-inter-miami" >leadup to Wednesday’s match</a> against Lionel Messi and Inter Miami.</p><p>His phone was, too.</p><p>“There has been just a massive outpouring of support and interest,” Baldwin told the Sun-Times on Wednesday morning, hours before the Blackhawks’ Patrick Kane led the pregame Sound the Alarm tradition. “The best example I can give you is my cell phone has been ringing off the hook for the last 24 hours, from local athletes and celebrities who want to sit down by the field today.”</p><p>The celebrity players mostly delivered.</p><p>The Fire’s Robert Lewandowski scored in the 10th minute and Inter Miami’s Casemiro converted a pinpoint Messi corner kick in the 48<sup>th</sup> during the 1-1 tie. In front of a franchise-record crowd of 63,094, Messi and Lewandowski both played the full 90 minutes and showed why the Fire and Major League Soccer have invested so heavily in marquee players.</p><p>As they proved, both Messi and Lewandowski can still play despite their advanced ages.</p><p>Messi (39) started slowly but got into the match late in the first half, eventually mustering four shots on target. He did have a chance for a dramatic winner in second-half stoppage time, but his free kick hit the Fire wall. Lewandowski (38) was generally held in check, but that was after he stuck out his right leg to turn in a precise Andrew Gutman cross for his sixth goal in nine MLS games.</p><p>“The assist, it was nice to get on it, but the finish was amazing,” Gutman said. “It’s kind of easy when you just put it in a spot and [Lewandowski] does the rest.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>KAMIL KRZACZYNSKI/Getty</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>And then there’s the other benefits, even though neither spoke to the media after the game.</p><p>With Lewandowski on the roster, the Fire are averaging 41,815 in three league matches at Soldier Field. Before Lewandowski, the Fire were drawing 19,668 over eight dates.</p><p>Wednesday was Messi’s second MLS game at Soldier Field. His first appearance — a 0-0 draw on April 13, 2025 — attracted 62,538. In 2023, Messi was injured and missed the Fire’s 4-1 win, but the event still drew 62,124 after an intense team marketing campaign.</p><p>On Wednesday, Messi was still quite the attraction but not the choice of most of the fans. Unlike last year’s Chicago game between the teams, the Fire had a slight majority of the customer support, many of whom booed Messi and chanted Lewandowski’s name. Lewandowski’s applause during pregame introductions was louder than Messi’s, and Inter Miami’s pink and black or Argentina’s light blue were easy to spot but didn’t overwhelm the Fire’s red or other home team paraphernalia.</p><p>The fan response Wednesday is one example of why it made sense for the Fire to go after Lewandowski during an already-strong season. Beyond his scoring, Lewandowski’s presence has given the Fire the type of figure to draw eyeballs from around the world.</p><p>It also presents logistical challenges similar to what Miami has dealt with during the Messi era. The Fire have had to handle increased ticket demand, the need for extra security and more media requests. Those are good problems to have.</p><p>Baldwin said MLS does well to share its best practices for these obstacles during regular calls between team presidents and quarterly Board of Governors meetings.</p><p>“Thankfully, this isn’t something that caught us flat-footed, as we had been recruiting Robert for a while,” Baldwin said. “That’s really exciting. It has lived up to the hype. There are a lot of fans who are very excited for Robert and for the club to be having the success we are.”</p>

entries.title: They fled the state to tie the knot. Sixty years later, my parents' love remains strong.
entries.summary: <p>This month my parents are beginning their seventh decade of marriage despite a law that tried to stop them.</p><p>Sixty years ago they were married in a church in Washington, D.C. They had to leave Maryland to do it. My mother is Black. My father is white. In Maryland their marriage was a crime.</p><p>They met in West Baltimore. Her city. Two student teachers at Harlem Park Junior High, the same classroom, one semester after the other.</p><p>They wrote each other every week that spring. Their students. Life back on campus. What they believed. When my mother came home to Baltimore for the summer, they were both seeing other people. They went on a date anyway.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-floatRight><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-cb0000" name="module-cb0000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnists bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2><br><i>In-depth political coverage, sports analysis, entertainment reviews and cultural commentary.</i><br></div> </div><p>That date was at the recently desegregated movie theater. They slipped in like racial fugitives. They found two empty seats. He walked down one aisle. She walked down the other. They sat side by side but didn't want their entrance or exit to cause a stir. They knew the looks wouldn't all come from white people. It was the summer of Black Power, after all.</p><p>My father proposed three times in two weeks. She turned him down twice. She was not being coy. What he asked was against the law. The third time she said yes.</p><p>My father's uncle told him he believed the love was real. Then he explained that if my father wanted to stay in the family, and in his grandfather's will, he would need to fall in love with someone else instead. Others said, "Think about what it will be like for the children."</p><p>They married two months later. They arrived at the church separately, the way a bride and groom do. This time it was tradition.</p><p>Afterward the caravan drove back to Baltimore with its headlights on. Cars on the highway pulled aside to let it pass. In the city people stopped walking to turn and stare and then pray for them. Men took off their hats. Everyone thought it was a funeral. The lights were only so nobody would get lost on the way to my grandparents' house in West Baltimore, where the reception was.</p><p>At the reception my father danced with my mother. He is red-headed and freckled and looks as English and Irish as he is. One woman watching them decided the groom had to be Black. Apparently she could not imagine a white boy dancing like that. My father was delighted.</p><p>Somewhere in there my father made her an offer. Jealous is a strange name to carry. He told her he would take hers instead. He would become Fred Todd.</p><p>She said no. She took the name Jealous.</p><p>Telling that used to make me chuckle. Who turns down any name for such a notorious adjective? I hear it a little differently now.</p><p>His grandfather had already disowned him and cut him out of the will. His own father had died years earlier from his third heart attack. My father was the eldest grandson of an industrialist. He had a great deal to lose and he lost all of it. His mother and his brothers stood by him. Much of the rest of the family did not. His name was the last thing that was his to give, and he offered to give that up too. She would not let him.</p><p>The following June the Supreme Court decided Loving v. Virginia. When my parents stood in that church, nobody knew it was coming. They married anyway.</p><p>They went West. With Loving grinding through the courts, they apparently decided the nation didn't need Jealous v. Maryland too.</p><p>San Diego first, then the Monterey Peninsula. There my father taught soldiers home from Vietnam, many of whom could not read. Later he founded a community where men learn to listen to one another, and to be listened to, most of them for the first time. My mother spent her career as a therapist. They raised us in California, far from her mother and her church and her city.</p><p>Every summer they sent me back east. Baltimore for her people. Maine for his. The move had cut them off from all of it. They handed it to me.</p><h3>Honoring love</h3><h3></h3><p>A decade ago, they returned to St. James Episcopal Church on Lafayette Square and renewed their vows for the 50th anniversary of Loving. My mother was baptized in that church. So was I. So was my son.</p><p>My mother wore the dress. Her grandmother sewed it for her in 1966, when my mother was 25. She sewed it for that church, where she worshiped. Then the law sent the wedding to Washington, and the dress never went down that aisle.</p><p>A half century later it did. My mother was crying. I told her to stop bragging. She looked at me, confused, tears still on her face. I told her she just wanted everybody to know it still fit.</p><p>Sixty years. My father is still the man who offered to give up his name. My mother is still the woman who would not let him.</p><p>They were never a test case. They were a marriage. They still are.</p><p>Happy anniversary, Mom and Dad. Thank you for being so courageous in love. My sister and I literally would never have existed but for it.</p><p><i>Ben Jealous is a professor of practice at the University of Pennsylvania and former president and CEO of the NAACP.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-ee0000" name="module-ee0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: License plate reader abuses worry conservatives too
entries.summary: <p>Last month, Texas Gov. Greg Abbott <a class="Link" href="https://www.texastribune.org/2026/08/28/texas-greg-abbott-flock-cameras-order-state-money/" target="_blank" >froze</a> state funding for automated license plate readers, acknowledging concerns about the warrantless surveillance enabled by such artificial intelligence-assisted cameras. Abbott took that step the day after Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis, a fellow Republican, <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2026/08/27/ron-desantis-says-flock-cameras-are-out-of-control-but-floridas-already-flooded-with-surveillance/" target="_blank" >declared</a> that license plate readers are "out of control."</p><p>Both governors cited recent reports about police officers <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2026/08/13/flock-cameras-and-license-plate-readers-are-everywhere-can-we-trust-cops-with-them/" target="_blank" >accused</a> of using license plate reader data for <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2026/07/10/florida-police-officer-used-mass-surveillance-network-to-stalk-romantic-interest/" target="_blank" >personal purposes</a>, which seem to be driving a <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2026/08/28/a-tale-of-two-moral-panics/" target="_blank" >shift</a> in public opinion about the technology. Such incidents highlight the perils of giving cops across the country easy access to such data, which they can use to track your travels, identify nearby vehicles and even predict your itinerary, without judicial oversight or meaningful internal supervision.</p><p>Abbott mentioned a Lufkin, Texas, police officer who was <a class="Link" href="https://www.kbtx.com/2026/08/27/officer-accused-using-flock-cameras-search-ex-girlfriends-plate-more-than-10000-times/" target="_blank" >charged</a> with using license plate reader information to stalk an ex-girlfriend, her relatives, and her acquaintances more than 10,000 times. DeSantis alluded to similar cases in Florida, where officers in <a class="Link" href="https://www.wfla.com/news/sarasota-county/sarasota-police-officer-accused-of-misusing-flock-databases-appears-in-court/" target="_blank" >Sarasota</a> and <a class="Link" href="https://www.wfla.com/news/polk-county/haines-city-officer-used-flock-cameras-to-track-estranged-wife-on-717-occasions-affidavit/" target="_blank" >Haines City</a> had recently been arrested for misusing license plate reader data.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-floatRight><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-f10000" name="module-f10000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnists bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2><br><i>In-depth political coverage, sports analysis, entertainment reviews and cultural commentary.</i><br></div> </div><p>"When I see, like, a police officer using this to track, like, an ex-girlfriend," DeSantis <a class="Link" href="https://www.wfla.com/news/florida/desantis-says-flock-cameras-are-out-of-control/" target="_blank" >said</a>, "I'm like, you know, what the hell's going on?" </p><p>Local officials are beginning to ask the same question.</p><p>As of Tuesday, the Institute for Justice <a class="Link" href="https://ij.org/institute-for-justice-unveils-new-database-tracking-cancelations-of-license-plate-reader-contracts/" target="_blank" >counted</a> 181 local governments that have canceled or declined to renew license plate reader contracts since the beginning of 2025. In Texas alone, the Dallas Express <a class="Link" href="https://dallasexpress.com/state/texas-cities-keep-dropping-flock-cameras-as-statewide-privacy-backlash-grows/" target="_blank" >reports</a>, at least 23 jurisdictions have dropped contracts, suspended service or reduced the size of their license plate reader networks.</p><p>Some <a class="Link" href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/10/us/flock-cameras-can-track-every-car-in-america-police-love-them-citizens-dont.html" target="_blank" >7,000</a> police departments have installed those networks, which include <a class="Link" href="https://deflock.org/" target="_blank" >around 140,000</a> cameras, without giving much thought to the privacy implications or the potential for abuse. But some of them are now having <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2026/08/31/the-belated-backlash-against-flock-cameras/" target="_blank" >second thoughts</a>, reflecting rising public skepticism of unconstrained license plate reader use.</p><p>In a YouGov <a class="Link" href="https://yougov.com/en-us/daily-results/20260824-a9b53-1" target="_blank" >survey</a> last month, 46% of respondents opposed police use of license plate readers, including 31% who were "strongly" opposed, while 38% favored the practice. A year ago, by contrast, YouGov <a class="Link" href="https://yougov.com/en-us/daily-results/20250904-67d37-1" target="_blank" >found</a> that 45% of Americans supported license plate readers, while 33% opposed them, including 20% who were "strongly" opposed.</p><p>That reversal coincides with <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2026/07/24/georgia-cops-keep-getting-arrested-for-misusing-flock-surveillance-data/" target="_blank" >proliferating</a> reports of <a class="Link" href="https://www.kake.com/news/crime/how-a-former-police-officer-used-a-security-system-to-stalk-his-wife/article_1e2df9e3-08fe-5f88-b13f-a3598c89ae5e.html" target="_blank" >blatant</a> license plate reader <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2026/09/02/wisconsin-cops-used-flock-over-100-times-to-track-a-navy-veteran-after-he-lawfully-recorded-a-traffic-stop/" target="_blank" >abuses</a>. The Institute for Justice has <a class="Link" href="https://ij.org/the-ij-database-of-alpr-abuse/" target="_blank" >identified</a> "well over 100" such incidents, which it notes "may be just the tip of the iceberg" given the reality of lax oversight and widespread data-sharing.</p><p>Police officers are supposed to use that information, which they can access on computers or mobile phones, only for legitimate law enforcement purposes. But as a Wichita police supervisor <a class="Link" href="https://www.yahoo.com/news/kansas-police-chief-used-flock-093300946.html" target="_blank" >conceded</a> in 2024, it's "not even possible" to enforce that policy by making sure that each search complies with it.</p><p>Compounding that challenge, each agency typically <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2026/07/31/kansas-lawsuit-alprs-turn-a-license-plate-into-the-functional-equivalent-of-a-gps-tracking-device/" target="_blank" >shares</a> license plate reader information with many others. Once that happens, The Wichita Eagle <a class="Link" href="https://www.govtech.com/public-safety/vehicle-surveillance-prompts-privacy-concerns-in-wichita-kan" target="_blank" >noted</a> in 2022, local police officials have "no control over how those outside agencies use it and no way to flag unlawful searches."</p><p>In Norfolk, Virginia, a local radio station <a class="Link" href="https://www.whro.org/virginia-center-for-investigative-journalism/2026-04-02/virginia-police-often-search-alpr-surveillance-data-for-vague-reasons/" target="_blank" >reported</a> last April, police officers often give "incomplete and imprecise reasons" for license plate reader searches, including "suspect," "suspicious" and "investigation" or "inv." Such vague labels hardly seem consistent with a <a class="Link" href="https://law.lis.virginia.gov/vacode/title2.2/chapter55.6/section2.2-5517/" target="_blank" >state law</a> requiring that cops state a "specific purpose," including "the offense type," thereby providing enough information to determine whether a search is legitimate.</p><p>"The police cannot police themselves," <a class="Link" href="https://ij.org/press-release/institute-for-justice-calls-flock-safetys-proposed-reforms-window-dressing/" target="_blank" >says</a> Institute for Justice attorney Robert Frommer. His organization <a class="Link" href="https://ij.org/issues/ijs-project-on-the-4th-amendment/license-plate-readers/" target="_blank" >argues</a> that a warrant generally should be required to access license plate reader data — a policy it aims to establish by <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2026/04/16/san-joses-creepy-and-deeply-intrusive-alpr-camera-system-is-unconstitutional-a-new-lawsuit-says/" target="_blank" >challenging</a> license plate reader networks on Fourth Amendment grounds and urging states to enact protective <a class="Link" href="https://ij.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/The-Automated-Surveillance-Accountability-and-Privacy-Act-V2.pdf" target="_blank" >legislation</a>.</p><p>The congressional response to license plate readers, including <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2026/09/03/a-new-bill-reflects-the-bipartisan-backlash-against-flock-enabled-mass-surveillance/" target="_blank" >several bills</a> and an investigation that Sen. Josh Hawley, R–Mo., <a class="Link" href="https://www.hawley.senate.gov/chairman-hawley-investigates-ai-powered-flock-cameras-amidst-privacy-concerns/" target="_blank" >announced</a> last month, has been dominated by conservative Republicans, which confirms that the backlash is not limited to libertarian or left-leaning critics. Whether it will yield <a class="Link" href="https://www.dailywire.com/news/the-texan-cure-for-high-tech-trespass" target="_blank" >effective constraints</a> is another question.</p><p>License plate reader are "easily containable," Abbott <a class="Link" href="https://www.texastribune.org/2026/08/28/texas-greg-abbott-flock-cameras-order-state-money/" target="_blank" >says</a>, a bit <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2026/08/27/getting-rid-of-flock-isnt-enough-to-solve-americas-surveillance-problem/" target="_blank" >overoptimistically</a>. "They're going to be required to be used responsibly if they're used at all."</p><p><i>Jacob Sullum is a senior editor at Reason magazine.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-890000" name="module-890000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Trump makes 9/11 about himself with lies
entries.summary: <p>There was a reason organizers of the 9/11 ceremony in Manhattan told President Donald Trump he could not speak at this year’s memorial service.</p><p>A good one, it turns out.</p><p>Because in a speech he gave Tuesday in Washington, he did exactly what they were presumably worried about — he made it about himself.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-floatRight><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-730000" name="module-730000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnists bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2><br><i>In-depth political coverage, sports analysis, entertainment reviews and cultural commentary.</i><br></div> </div><p>According to <a class="Link" href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/27/us/politics/trump-911-pentagon-ground-zero.html" target="_blank" >The New York Times</a>, Trump had wanted a speaking role at the service, but the national Sept. 11 Memorial and Museum, which oversees the site, said no, as they’ve maintained for the last decade-plus that the venue and event should be nonpartisan.</p><p>Trump has long used awful tragedies to either puff himself up, trash political opponents, or sell lies to the American people.</p><p>He blamed a deadly plane crash at Reagan National Airport last year on diversity, equity and inclusion policies. He blamed Puerto Ricans for the devastation they endured after Hurricane Maria in 2017. He reportedly considered withholding disaster relief after the California wildfires based on the way affected regions voted. In an interview on Fox News meant to commemorate the 75th anniversary of D-Day in Normandy, he used the occasion to slam former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi … with graves of the dead behind him.</p><p>And now, with the 25th anniversary of what many New Yorkers consider the darkest day in modern history, Trump has done it again.</p><p>He told a rambling, nonsensical story — one he’s told before — about going to ground zero just after terrorists flew two commercial jets into the twin towers. In the story, which no one has been able to verify, despite multiple attempts, he says firefighters had to carry him out of One Liberty Plaza, also known as the U.S. Steel Building, because they thought it was about to collapse.</p><p>As CNN fact checker Daniel Dale <a class="Link" href="https://x.com/ddale8/status/2097361398984741326?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw%7Ctwcamp%5Etweetembed%7Ctwterm%5E2097361398984741326%7Ctwgr%5E94e986be1f931d420ab07fd53f313a6ccee55ded%7Ctwcon%5Es1_&ref_url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.mediaite.com%2Fpolitics%2Ftrump%2Ftrump-makes-wild-new-claim-in-rambling-remarks-about-visiting-9-11-rubble%2F" target="_blank" >notes</a>, there’s no evidence Trump went into this building, especially at a time when NYPD and FDNY had locked down the area. There’s no evidence that building was collapsing — in fact, it was deemed structurally sound and reopened within two months of the attacks. There’s no evidence he was carried out of it by firefighters.</p><p>But the lie isn’t even the worst part. Pretend it was all true — why would the leader of our country, and a New Yorker, decide to make that tragic day about himself?</p><p>Because that’s who Trump is. He’s a malignant narcissist.</p><p>He’s also, incidentally, a terrible and ineffectual president, who’s made ill-fated decisions that he has to keep defending, and there’s nothing he won’t do to make himself look and feel better.</p><p>Within the first two minutes of his speech, he was cravenly using 9/11 to justify and promote his dumb war in Iran — two events separated by 25 years and 6,000 miles.</p><p>“And I will tell you, we’re right now fighting because we have a certain nation that wanted a nuclear weapon, they were very close to getting it, and now they have no chance at getting it. They will never have a nuclear weapon. Iran will not have a nuclear weapon. And they’ve been punished greatly. As you know, we’ve really taken it to them.”</p><p>As a New Yorker who lived through 9/11, still one of the worst days of my life, I’m utterly sickened by Trump’s crass, political and self-promotional framing of that awful day.</p><p>And I’m relieved he won’t be given a platform to do it again on Friday’s anniversary in lower Manhattan.</p><p>Because for Trump, everything is his for the taking, and absolutely nothing is sacred.</p><p><i>S.E. Cupp is the host of “S.E. Cupp Unfiltered” on CNN.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-9c0000" name="module-9c0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Dear Abby: Spoiled brother in his 60s causing trouble for the rest of the family
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I have a younger brother who has moved back to the area where the rest of our siblings live. He went for 30 years without keeping in close contact with anyone during that time. He's the youngest of 10 children, and our mother spoiled him rotten. He's in his 60s now and still acts like an immature spoiled child. Our father had to bail him out of financial situations more times than I can count. Despite that, he hated our father and announced it when he came home for Dad's funeral.</p><p>The problem we're having now is that he constantly tries to stir up problems between the rest of us. Until he returned, we were a close-knit family. None of my other family members want anything to do with him, and they refuse invitations to get together if he will be there.</p><p>Abby, I love my brother, but I'm tired of his behavior. He had a drug problem when he lived out of state. He claims he's clean now, but he has now replaced the drugs with alcohol. How can I get my family back without him if he isn't willing to admit he is the problem? — <i>SIBLING SITUATION IN WISCONSIN</i></p><p><b>DEAR SIBLING:</b> Stop inviting your brother to these gatherings. The sooner you do, the sooner he will learn the consequences of trying to stir up trouble among the siblings. Unless there are consequences for his behavior, it won't stop. His behavior isn't unusual for an addict. By that, I mean it is common for an addict to replace his drug addiction with another one and even more common to deny having a problem.</p><p>There's a program that was created decades ago called Al-Anon. Al-Anon (al-anon.org) is an offshoot of Alcoholics Anonymous, created for anyone who is affected by a loved one's drinking. It holds meetings everywhere, and you should have no trouble locating one near you. Attend some of those meetings, which are free of charge. When you do, you will meet others with problems similar to the one you are having.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I have been planning a dream trip to Europe with some family members. The people I'm traveling with are young and like to take selfies everywhere, which takes a lot of time. I don't care about doing that type of thing. They are "girly girls," and I am plain. I never know what to do while they are doing these things. They love hair and makeup and take up valuable time with these activities. I don't begrudge them this, but do you have any advice on what to say or do while I wait around? — <i>FRETTING THIS TRIP</i></p><p><b>DEAR FRETTING:</b> When people take selfies as they travel, part of the fun is capturing themselves against picturesque landscapes, famous landmarks or works of art. If you don't want to be in the photos, keeping a visual record of your journey can still be fulfilling. Develop your photo or video skills by focusing on the scenery the girls are using as backdrops. If you are artistically inclined, a sketchbook may be more your speed. If images aren't your thing, bring a travel journal in which you can jot down your impressions and favorite aspects of the places you visit.</p><p><i>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren. For nearly four decades, Jeanne Phillips penned this column, which was founded in 1956 by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 270135, Kansas City, MO 64127.</i></p>
entries.author: Abigail Van Buren

entries.title: Playoff loss to Rams haunts, propels Bears QB Caleb Williams into new season
entries.summary: <p>In the middle of a conversation that wandered from blueberries and organic bread recipes to iconic sports leaders like Derek Jeter and Michael Jordan, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> quarterback Caleb Williams landed on one of his least favorite topics.</p><p>For every amazing thing that happened last season, including his own heroic plays and overall growth, the bitterness of losing to the Rams in the playoffs sticks with him.</p><p>His <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/01/18/bears-qb-caleb-williams-forces-overtime-with-ridiculous-pass-but-rams-win-20-17" >ridiculous touchdown pass to tight end Cole Kmet</a> to tie that game in the final minute and force overtime was the most amazing play of the NFL season. Williams got the snap at the Rams’ 20-yard line, scrambled back to the 40 to buy time as their pass rushers chased him and got hit as he heaved it to the left corner of the end zone for Kmet’s over-the-shoulder catch.</p><p>Even on rewatch, it’s hard to believe he put that ball on target.</p><p>The highlight has 1.2 million views on the NFL’s YouTube page. The iPhone video shot from that corner by NFL Network reporter Stacey Dales is at 5.6 million and counting. And Williams would rather not see it again anytime soon, given that the game ended when he threw an interception in overtime and the Rams won with a field goal.</p><p>“It burns,” he said toward the end of training camp. “It’s frustrating. It still bothers me today. Every single time the play pops up... it feels like it was for nothing.”</p><p>That’s the emotional reaction. He usually pivots next to introspection and a bigger-picture view. Reaching the divisional round of the playoffs and getting that close to advancing was a step, both for him as a young player and a franchise that hadn’t made it that deep in the playoffs in 15 years.</p><p>But even with a broader perspective, steps only matter if they continue forward. The Bears are looking for the year-over-year momentum that fuels NFL powerhouses and they need to keep climbing when this season starts Sunday at the Panthers.</p><p>They got better in every way under coach Ben Johnson last season.</p><p>His precision, drive and competence was a sharp turn from predecessors Matt Eberflus and Matt Nagy. While Williams still has significant work to do, he set the franchise’s single-season passing record and spurred general manager Ryan Poles to start planning for a contract extension. They won the NFC North for the first time since 2018.</p><p>Everything about last season was progress. Now there must be more of it.</p><p>Williams is ambivalent when it comes to recognizing the Bears’ overall path versus feeling the pain of that loss. He believes in pressing on at all times, which served him well during a tumultuous rookie season. He’s also the guy who bristles when he sees Tulane’s angry little wave logo because he still hates that at USC he lost to the school in the 2022 Cotton Bowl.</p><p>“I’m not a person who holds onto those moments where I’m stuck in a rut,” he explained. “It’s going to sting every time it comes back up, but it doesn’t get me into a funk... We’re onto the next and we’re going to focus on [going] further than we did last year.”</p><p>Williams has more influence on whether that happens than anyone at Halas Hall. Even Johnson can’t win without a quarterback.</p><p>The lasting images of his 2025 season are the throw to Kmet, the fourth-and-eight jump pass in the playoff win over the Packers, the walk-off touchdown pass to DJ Moore to beat the Packers in the regular season and various other jaw-dropping scrambles and passes. Those plays meant so much that the details sometimes got lost in the shuffle.</p><p>Not to Johnson, of course. He kept it real with Williams about his decision making, errors in his footwork that led to inaccurate throws and anticipating defensive coverages. Tightening things up in those three areas would make things “significantly different in terms of our passing game,” Johnson told the Sun-Times.</p><p>The Bears were 10th in passing offense last season, which was their best since 2013, but Johnson only ever thinks about finishing No. 1. He obsesses over Lombardi Trophies and scoring records. Placing 10th doesn’t do anything for him.</p><p>Johnson set the bar at completing 70% of his passes, and Williams finished last in the league at 58.1%, to which Johnson said 70% is “what elite passing offenses do, and we were far from that.” Then he took Williams through every pass play from the season and showed him how 70% would’ve been possible. That also would have elevated his 90.1 passer rating, which was 22nd in the NFL.</p><p>Becoming the quarterback Johnson believes he can be is the best way for Williams to move forward. It would turn the pain of losing to the Rams into a stepping stone. What he does this season will determine whether that was as good as it gets for the Bears or the starting point for something so much better.</p>
entries.author: Jason Lieser

entries.title: ‘Zero fights’ at a Chicago teen beach gathering, but some adults left youth feeling discouraged
entries.summary: <p>Around 5:30 p.m. Aug. 19, more than 160 Chicago teenagers were hanging out, eating food and taking photos at North Avenue Beach.</p><p>Then the volleyball players came.</p><p>The beach party — permitted by the city — had signs around the courts. Teens were throwing footballs and playing field games. Despite teens and adults asking the players to hold their games until after the event ended at 7 p.m., the players continued setting up for their regularly scheduled games.</p><p>The conflict was resolved peacefully, but it was more than a mix-up over beach courts. Some teens said the encounter left them feeling discouraged and unwelcome in a public space they had gone through the proper channels to reserve.</p><p>For some of the teens and the adults who organized the beach hangout, it raised a larger question: Who is actually welcome in Chicago's public spaces?</p><p>The encounter comes as Chicago grapples with how to make public spaces safer and more welcoming for young people while responding to concerns about violence, property damage and large teen gatherings.</p><p>Viral social media posts and news coverage showing large teen trends, gatherings and “takeovers” have fueled debates about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/06/16/ald-ray-lopez-parental-responsibility-ordinance-city-council" target="_blank" ><u>parent accountability ordinances</u></a>, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/01/06/mayor-brandon-johnson-revised-curfew-measure-opposition-brian-hopkins-rockin-new-years-eve" target="_blank" ><u>snap curfews</u></a>, escort policies and other approaches to managing youth gatherings.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" their homes. But for teen and youth organizers, the challenge isn't only creating those spaces — it's making sure young people feel that they are actually welcome in them.</p><p>On Aug. 19, Project Exploration, a local youth development nonprofit organization, worked with the Mayor’s Office of Education, Youth and Human Services to throw the beach party for South Side and West Side youths.</p><p>Austin resident Carla Jones, 18, was one of 20 Project Exploration youth employees who helped organize the event.</p><p>“We thought of everything teens would want to do — volleyball, we had the game trucks, the selfie booth,” Jones said.</p><p>Janeicia Williams, who helped oversee the project, said the gathering was also about something less tangible: giving young people a chance to occupy a public space without feeling like they had to justify being there.</p><p>“There aren’t a lot of times that we get to be in these spaces,” said Williams, director of community ecosystem at Project Exploration.</p><p>The mayor’s office invested more than $10,000 for food, transportation, the video game truck, a handwashing station, portable toilet, tables and chairs.</p><div class="Enhancement" The only thing we did was pay for some stuff and put in some booking information.”</p><p>Upon arrival at the beach party, attendees had to register and go through a security check before enjoying lunch, music and games.</p><p>“We wanted to create a safe space for the kids so that they end the summer off with a nice event before they go back to school,” said Austin resident Porschay Graham, 19.</p><p>For some of Chicago’s Black and Brown teenagers from the South and West sides, the party was a chance to experience a part of their own city they had never explored. they understood that. There was a certain level of entitlement.”</p><p>Jones said she felt the teens were misunderstood.</p><p>“When we're actually trying to show that teens are not all about violence and ruckus or when we're making events for teens to feel safe,” Jones said. “It's kind of discouraging.”</p><p>Williams said the moment felt like a big inconvenience for some of the players.</p><p>Williams saw the encounter as part of a larger question about how Black teenagers are perceived in public spaces.</p><p>“If the roles were reversed and it was a bunch of Black kids trying to take over that part of the beach, there probably would have been more problems,” Williams said. “It probably would have been police called.”</p><p>Williams’ concern points to another tension the city is trying to navigate: how to create more places for young people to gather without treating every large gathering as a potential threat.</p><p>On June 24, City Council members <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/06/24/teen-takeovers-chicago-city-council-hearing-youth-testimony" target="_blank" ><u>held a public hearing</u></a> where teens testified about “teen takeovers.” During the hearing, the Office of Community Safety and the Office of Education and Youth Policy reported “49 teen trends” in June. Shine On Chicago</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>“We would like to see more people raise their hand to say, ‘Hey, we'll open up our space — we'll open up our business — late for a poetry event,'” Humphries said.</p><p>Creating those opportunities can be complicated, particularly when residents and business owners have also experienced the disruption that can come with large youth gatherings.</p><p>Humphries said changing the perception about these gatherings requires adults to see young people as more than an inconvenience or source of disruption — they need to remember that they were once teens.</p><p>For Williams, supporting Chicago’s young people requires surrounding them with caring adults and activities that youth are actually interested in.</p><p>“Even when planning this (beach party) — if I'm being very quite frank — it was very uncomfortable,” Williams said. “Any large-scale group of people without parameters or certain logistics or certain controls in place can get out of hand.”</p><p>The August beach gathering ended peacefully, with teens spending the afternoon playing games, dancing to the DJ and meeting new and old friends from across Chicago.</p><p>For Williams, that was the point of the event.</p><p>“There were absolutely zero fights, there were zero weapons, there were zero altercations,” Williams said. “Young people — especially young Black people — are not a threat to the peace that we see here every day.”</p>

entries.title: In Englewood, a new sculpture park blooms with murals, vivid color and hope for 'good things'
entries.summary: <p>On a recent weekday morning, there’s a buzz of activity along Englewood’s 63rd Street between May Street and Racine Avenue. Today, this corner is brimming with oversized drum sculptures, colorful murals that stretch the length of the property and a series of star-shaped artworks.</p><p>It’s all part of a new sculpture park, courtesy of the artist-driven <a class="Link" href="https://englewoodartscollective.org/" target="_blank" ><u>Englewood Arts Collective</u></a>. The group soft-launched the public art installation in August and will host activities here this weekend in alignment with the annual <a class="Link" href="https://www.instagram.com/englewoodmusicfest" target="_blank" ><u>Englewood Music Festival</u></a>. Over the next three to five years, the collective plans to fill this once-vacant lot with art and give neighbors a place of beauty to gather in.</p><p>As the train whirs by, cicadas hum and a team of lawnmowers meticulously cut the grass, Janell Nelson, the collective’s director and cofounder, walks through the space, wearing an orange T-shirt that says “joy builder” on the back. That’s Nelson’s M.O.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-e10000" name="image-e10000"></a> The Stories of Us. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Jeremy Battle/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Nelson and her fellow Englewood-rooted artists who are part of the collective will also once again host a stage and arts village inside the music festival.</p><p>The sculpture park is the latest initiative since the collective — made up of 10 artists, including MacArthur Genius Grant winner <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/arts/2025/10/08/macarthur-genius-grant-winners-2025-tonika-lewis-johnson-englewood-folded-map-project-tommy-orange" target="_blank" ><u>Tonika Lewis Johnson</u></a> — launched nearly a decade ago. It’s all rooted in rewriting the narrative of the South Side neighborhood, where members of the collective grew up.</p><p>“We were faced with what was going on in the media and what they chose to highlight,” said collective member David Robinson, aka Rob Smooth, a 53-year-old producer and artist. “So we sought out to change that narrative by making sure when you Google Englewood, a lot of good things would come up related to art, culture, film, music.”</p><p>Collective members say art has always had a home in Englewood. That includes esteemed saxophonist Ernest Dawkins’ longstanding <a class="Link" href="https://englewoodjazzfestival.org/" target="_blank" ><u>Englewood Jazz Festival</u></a>, which will take place Sept. 17-19.</p><p>In recent years, the collective also hosted a studio and exhibition pop-up in collaboration with the chamber of commerce, provided direct financial support to artists and organized skill-building workshops. This latest effort is about bringing beauty and foot traffic to the 63rd Street corridor.</p><p>Like other South and West side neighborhoods, Englewood has faced ongoing disinvestment. The sculpture park sits just blocks from the former Whole Foods, a once-heralded economic improvement catalyst that ultimately <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/culture-the-arts/2022/11/13/englewood-whole-foods-closes-november-13-2022" target="_blank" ><u>closed in 2022</u></a> after only six years in the neighborhood.</p><div celebration recognized <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/arts/2026/07/02/milton-mizenburg-artist-pocket-garden-oakland-southeast-side" target="_blank" ><u>artist Milton Mizenburg Jr.</u></a> and his sculptures on view in a garden in Oakland, a pocket community just north of Kenwood and east of Bronzeville. Both that display and the one in Englewood are a testament to art’s ability to transform public spaces.</p><p>As visitors enter the Englewood park along May Street, they pass by a mirrored gate, which Nelson said is a hat tip to Chicago’s famous “Bean” in Millennium Park, but also, “a reflection of our love for the community. It's a reflection of the people that live here.”</p><p>A gravel path leads past the <a class="Link" href="https://www.themagnificentmile.com/everybody-is-a-star-on-the-mag-mile" target="_blank" ><u>painted star sculptures</u></a>, which the Magnificent Mile Association commissioned the collective to create for an installation along Michigan Avenue last year. Now, the colorful works by six Chicago artists have a new home.</p><p>Deeper inside the park sit five oversized painted drums, part of the national touring show known as <a class="Link" href="https://www.thestoriesofus.org/" target="_blank" ><u>The Stories of Us</u></a>. Each of the works reflect on America and its past as the nation turns 250 years old. One of the drums, painted by <a class="Link" href="https://youtu.be/P-KnNes8rXw" target="_blank" ><u>collective member Pugs Atomz</u></a>, wrestles with the history of the U.S. Census, especially in Black neighborhoods like Englewood. class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Hector Gonzalez, the project and site manager, said he this project as an investment in the neighborhood’s youth. “That’s in the back of my head, always, is providing something that kids can look up to and be like, ‘oh wow. That’s for me, in my neighborhood,’” he said. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Jeremy Battle/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Now, as an adult, he sees projects like this as an investment in the neighborhood’s youth.</p><p>“That's in the back of my head, always, is providing something that kids can look up to and be like, ‘oh wow. That's for me, in my neighborhood, and I don't have to go out to Downtown or Lincoln Park,’” Gonzalez said. “And they feel happy and excited about it, and they're proud to be where they come from.”</p><p>The transformation of the space was funded primarily through grants from groups like the Chicago Community Trust and <a class="Link" href="https://driehausfoundation.org/news/2026/support-for-emerging-artists-historic-garden-and-mental-health-resources-for-journalists-included-in-summer-awards" target="_blank" ><u>Driehaus Foundation</u></a>.</p><p>At the center of the garden, there’s a spot that Nelson said has been left intentionally blank — it’s her way of leaving room for whatever comes next. But in the meantime, Nelson says with pride, “Our soft launch went hard.”</p><p><i>Courtney Kueppers is an arts and culture reporter at WBEZ.</i></p>

16, 19-20</p><p>Chicago isn’t the only city in Illinois teeming with talent. The Oak Park Film Festival will illustrate that point by celebrating the wealth of actors, directors and writers from the west suburb. The event begins with a showing of Nicole Holofcener’s 2013 film, “Enough Said,” followed by a video interview with cast member and Oak Park Native Tavi Gevinson. The rest of the schedule is populated with documentaries, such as Dan Greenstone and Travis Chandler’s 81-minute “Surviving Zenkik Farm,” which focuses on former members of a commune who are working to rebuild their lives, a list that includes an Oak Park resident. Among the short nonfiction films is Brian Zahm's "Abel," about a photographer who suddenly lost his sight, and Risé A Sanders-Weir’s “Be the People,” which profiles six Oak Park residents trying to better their community. Illinois St.<br><b>When: </b>Sept. 17-20</p><p>Full-length documentary may be the least-populated category at the fest this year, but the three entries are diverse and compelling. Amita Arudpragasam’s “Thayakam (Motherland)” explores climate crisis in Sri Lanka, while Shashwati Talukdar’s “Marriage Cops” features officers-turned-relationship counselors in northern India. In “The Energy That Heals,” Christina Vircillo Bresson examines the science of bodily restoration. The short film category is another highlight, as many filmmakers have offered dynamic stories in small packages. For example, there’s a drama that features a crime lord and his wife in a dimly lit bathroom (“What Remains of Us”), an animated film about how Muslim parents discuss sex with their kids (“Halal Bodies”) and a documentary that revisits a Nepali immigrant’s lawsuit against the state of Mississippi (“Threading the American Dream”). The sole entry from a local filmmaker comes from Northwestern University student Shreya Saini, whose short, “Meethi,” uses the preparation of food to tackle themes of love and grief. <i>Tickets $5+. State St.<br><b>When: </b>Nov. 6-15</p><p>The fest returns for a 32nd year with two standout, full-length documentaries. Louis Massiah and Monica Henriquez’s “Toni Cade Bambara School of Organizing” spotlights the career of the filmmaker, writer and activist, who was an influential figure in contemporary Black literature. Also featured is “Abanitu: A family documentary” by Brooke C. Obie, who is known for her TV/film newsletter, “Black Girl Watching.” Obie’s film takes a multifaceted look at her family’s stewardship of their ancestral land in North Carolina. Multiple selections by Chicago filmmakers are included in the fest’s “From the Block” showcase. entries.title: Chicago artist Tony Fitzpatrick’s memory lives on in final film role, directed by his children
entries.summary: <p>Tony Fitzpatrick only appears in “Driven” for a brief time, but he approached his kids’ short film as if it were a big-budget production.</p><p>He was serious and focused, running his lines until the last minute. And he took the time to shake hands with everyone on set, praising their efforts.</p><p>It would be the final role for the beloved Chicago visual artist, actor, writer and gallerist, who <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2025/10/11/chicago-artist-tony-fitzpatrick-dead-66-steppenwolf" target="_blank" ><u>died at 66 from a heart attack</u></a> last October – just several months after filming. Though Fitzpatrick was mostly known for his whimsical mixed-media collages, drawings and paintings, he also appeared in high-profile films, including <b>“</b>Philadelphia,” “Chi-Raq” and “Primal Fear.”</p><p>“He couldn’t stop telling us how proud he was of us,” said his daughter, Gabrielle Fitzpatrick, 31, who wrote and directed “Driven” with her brother, Max Fitzpatrick, 34. Both appear in the film.</p><p>“We would have loved to continue directing him [in other films], but it's really beautiful in the sense that it felt like him passing his gifts on to us.”</p><div Dogs” and “The Godfather” on a camcorder.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Candace Dane Chambers/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>The 12-minute film will premiere at the <a class="Link" href="https://cuff.org/" target="_blank" ><u>Chicago Underground Film Festival</u></a> in three sold-out showings at Harper Theater in Hyde Park on Sept. 24 and Sept. 26-27. It follows a Chicago rideshare driver, portrayed by Max, as he picks up customers, grapples with heartbreak and rejection, and listens to increasingly harmful rhetoric from a self-help podcaster.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/art/2025/12/20/tony-fitzpatrick-black-swan-elegies-art-west-town" >Chicagoans pay homage to artist Tony Fitzpatrick: ‘Tony was fiercely proud of Chicago’</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>It is the first film that the siblings and up-and-coming filmmakers have directed together. They shot in Chicago with a mostly local cast and crew, including executive producer Paolo Lopez, producer and co-writer Caleb Sanabria, assistant director Louie Morco and director of photography Nick Emmanuele.</p><p>Inspired by some of Max’s experiences, the film demonstrates how influencers can take advantage of people who already feel isolated, pushing them further away from others.</p><p>“Driven” has moments that may remind viewers of the male loneliness epidemic or the “manosphere,” an online community of influencers promoting misogynistic views. But Max and Gabrielle said the film’s message applies to everyone.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a degree from Columbia College Chicago.</p><p>“There's a lot of toxic stuff on the internet for everybody. When you're alone, you turn to these things on social media, and you're getting exploited by voices telling you how to live. And in the end, it's kind of a grand scheme for you to buy products.”</p><p>Max’s character’s social interaction is limited to brief conversations with unhelpful friends, women on dating apps and his passengers, two of whom are played by his sister and his father.</p><p>“Some of the best movies that he got to do in his career were bit parts, but very memorable,” Max said. “He showed that you can put your thumbprint on a project no matter how big or small the role.”</p><p>Before his death, Fitzpatrick was able to see a rough cut of the film, which also includes shots of Chicago landmarks. Locals will recognize the Diversity Rock ‘N’ Bowl sign,<b> </b><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/murals-mosaics/2022/12/16/23506555/chicago-murals-paschke-ed-jefferson-park-lawrence-avenue" target="_blank" ><u>Jefferson Park murals by Ed Paschke</u></a>,<b> </b>one of Fitzpatrick’s mentors,<b> </b>and the Heart O’ Chicago Motel sign, which is featured in Fitzpatrick’s work.</p><p>“This is a love letter to my dad,” Max said. “If you look at his artwork, there's the solid subject that's in the middle, but then there’s a whole universe surrounding the piece. Following the film festival, they hope to land “Driven” on a streaming platform and film both a narrative feature and documentary based on their father. They also want to create a retrospective exhibition featuring his art.</p><p>“For some time, Max and I were trying to get jobs in film with mixed success,” said Gabrielle, of Ukrainian Village, who studied international relations in Italy and gained some hands-on film experience at a program in Mexico.<b> </b></p><p>“I think something just broke in our brains – or maybe was fixed in our brains – and we just said, ‘No one's going to hand us anything. We have to go out there and make something for ourselves.’ That is the ethos that we were raised with. entries.title: What is NITA, Chicago's new transit agency tasked with reforming CTA/Metra/Pace?
entries.summary: <p>The Northern Illinois Transit Authority’s board meets for the first time Thursday, officially launching the agency tasked with transforming Chicago-area public transit.</p><p>NITA replaces the Regional Transportation Authority, which had governed CTA, Metra and Pace since 1974.</p><p>The reshaping of public transit began last year when lawmakers <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/springfield/2025/10/30/mass-transit-funding-legislation-chicago-illinois-general-assembly-fiscal-cliff-cta-metra-pace" target="_blank" >passed the NITA bill overnight</a> on Halloween. It was a last-minute, $1.5 billion bailout to save the agencies from service cuts. The NITA law also restructured transit governance, aiming to elevate CTA, Metra and Pace into world-class services.</p><p>Here's what you need to know about NITA:</p><h3>What will NITA do?</h3><p>NITA has several requirements and a timeline to complete them.</p><p>Here's what the agency must do:<br></p><ul class="rte2-style-ul" id="rte-f68d13a0-abbf-11f1-87e3-65c3227503c9"><li>“Unify” fares by 2030. This will eliminate needing to buy a second ticket at full price to transfer from, say, Metra to CTA.</li><li>Coordinate service. The RTA had limited power to ensure bus and rail service overlapped in a way that made sense. NITA, however, can plan service, bus and rail investments, and set fares.</li><li>Vote next June on whether to create a transit police department. Cook County Sheriff Tom Dart is leading a task force to research the issue. He has <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/transportation/2026/06/25/cook-county-sheriff-tom-dart-nita-cita-metra-pace-police" target="_blank" >said it would be an easy</a>, though costly, option.</li><li>Deploy trained customer service representatives called "transit ambassadors" by July 2027.</li><li>Mandate electric buses. The law prohibits CTA and Pace from buying any new gas-powered buses, with a few exceptions.</li><li>Create a system to develop property near transit hubs. NITA has new powers to buy and sell land to encourage "transit-oriented development," the idea that walkable property near transit ought to be used for people and business.</li></ul><h3>Why NITA?</h3><p>NITA was born out of an impending financial disaster.</p><p>Chicago's transit agencies were <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/transportation/2025/03/21/cta-metra-pace-rta-service-cuts-financial-crisis-commuting-transportation" target="_blank" >headed for a “fiscal cliff.”</a> They predicted 40% cuts to bus and rail service — the result of low ridership, inadequate funding and dwindling pandemic relief grants.</p><p>Illinois lawmakers said they could deliver $1.5 billion more each year for transit. But first they demanded reform. Under the RTA system, the CTA, Metra and Pace often competed against each other for riders and funds.</p><p>Some lawmakers proposed combining them into a single agency. Others took a cue from a research trip to Munich, Germany. They proposed strengthening Chicago transit's umbrella organization, the RTA, to control service and make the agencies work together.</p><p>The second idea won. Gov. JB Pritzker <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/transportation/2025/12/16/illinois-transit-bill-signed-pritzker" target="_blank" >signed the NITA Act</a> in December.</p><h3>What has NITA changed already?</h3><p>NITA, the agency, is new. But the law behind it has already pumped in millions of dollars to transit since it first took effect June 1.</p><p>Much of that money has gone to public safety.</p><p>One of the RTA’s last acts was directing transit agencies <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/transportation/2026/03/19/rta-nita-board-security-survey-cta-metra-pace" target="_blank" >to make security improvements</a>. A public survey revealed it a top priority of riders. Millions of dollars have been spent on <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/transportation/2026/04/16/rta-nita-lsecurity-service-cta-metra-pace" target="_blank" >increased CTA patrols</a> by Chicago police, sheriff’s deputies and private K9 security.</p><p>The money is also improving bus and rail service.</p><p>The CTA <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/transportation/2026/08/18/cta-requent-bus-network-fullerton-35th-central" target="_blank" >added bus routes</a> to its Frequent Network, and it's <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/fran-spielman-show/2025/11/06/cta-interim-president-nora-leerhsen-orange-line-midway-airport-24-hour-service-mass-transit-bailout" target="_blank" >planning 24-hour Orange Line service</a> to Midway. Metra <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/transportation/2026/05/27/metra-train-rock-island-joliet" target="_blank" >added trains</a> to some of its southern lines. Pace has also <a class="Link" href="https://www.pacebus.com/mayjune-2026-service-improvements" target="_blank" >added</a> bus service.</p><h3>Who’s paying?</h3><p>New money for transit comes from a couple sources:<br></p><ul class="rte2-style-ul" id="rte-f68d13a1-abbf-11f1-87e3-65c3227503c9"><li>Nearly a half billion dollars comes from a quarter-percent hike in the Chicago region’s RTA sales tax.</li><li>Nearly a billion dollars comes from shifting most of the state’s sales tax on motor fuel to public transit. The money used to go to the state’s Road Fund. To compensate, the NITA law let the Illinois Tollway <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/transportation/2026/08/19/illinois-tollway-toll-hike" target="_blank" >raise tolls</a> for the first time in over a decade.</li></ul><h3>Who runs NITA?</h3><p>The NITA board has 20 directors appointed by the governor, mayor of Chicago, Cook County board president and the five collar counties. Most of those directors serve dual roles on the boards of CTA, Metra and Pace. That reduces the total number of board members from 47, under the RTA, to 33.</p><p>NITA has some familiar faces.</p><p>Mayor Brandon Johnson appointed CTA chair Lester Barclay to the NITA board. He's an attorney who has publicly questioned NITA's increased control of the CTA. Cook County Board President Toni Preckwinkle chose former RTA director Tom Kotarac for the CTA and NITA boards. Kotarac has been leading a NITA transition committee. Former RTA Chairman Kirk Dillard will not take a NITA board seat.</p><p>The NITA system notably shifts power from Johnson. The mayor used to appoint a majority of the CTA’s seven-member board. Under NITA, the mayor picks three.</p><p>The NITA board is scheduled Thursday to select a chairman and interim executive director. The board is also set to vote on a system-wide low-income reduced fare program, and to expand the student pass to work year-round.</p>
