entries.title: Southwest Side veteran Ald. Matt O'Shea will call it quits after four terms
entries.summary: <p>Bemoaning how the job of a City Council member has changed, Ald. Matt O’Shea, who helped to lead the budget rebellion against Mayor Brandon Johnson, is calling it quits after four terms.</p><p>After 16 years as alderperson and 30 as a community leader in the Far Southwest Side neighborhoods of Beverly and Morgan Park, O’Shea (19th) said it’s time for him to “step back and do something else.”</p><p>“To do this job right, it’s more than a full-time job. You don’t have days off. You can’t go to the grocery store. If there’s a crime pattern or something happening in the neighborhood, it’s very stressful. You have to be out front," said O’Shea, who is endorsing his chief of staff Erin Ross as his replacement.</p><p>“This job takes a lot out of you and it’s only fair to your community to give it everything you have. You start to think, `I don’t know if I can continue giving at that level.’ So it’s time to step out.”</p><p>O’Shea, 57, is the third Council member to choose political retirement over a reelection bid. <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/fran-spielman-show/2026/07/08/one-of-mayor-brandon-johnson-most-ardent-city-council-adversaries-wont-seek-reelection-in-2027" >Ald. Marty Quinn </a>(13th), another outspoken mayoral critic, and Workforce Development Committee Chair <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/fran-spielman-show/2026/09/09/ald-mike-rodriguez-22nd-ward-not-seeking-re-election-brandon-johnson-city-council-ally" >Mike Rodriguez</a> (22nd), a Johnson ally, are also leaving the City Council.</p><p>A former social worker-turned aldermanic aide, O’Shea was one of 13 new members sworn into office along with then-Mayor Rahm Emanuel in 2011.</p><p>Since then, the City Council has taken a sharp left turn with seven Democratic Socialists serving alongside Johnson, the most liberal mayor in Chicago history.</p><p>That philosophical change has dramatically altered the role of a Chicago alderperson from what O’Shea believes it should be.</p><p>“We spend a lot more time now down at City Hall and you can start to lose touch… You need to be in the neighborhood. You need to have eyes on things. You need to be visiting your schools and parks, driving your commercial strips, communicating with your business community — and you’re not able to do as much of that,” O’Shea told the Sun-Times.</p><p>“You’re finding information out second-hand. Instead of today, you get a call tomorrow and you’re like, 'Damn it. I should have been there.’“</p><p>O’Shea blamed the social isolation brought on by the pandemic and the civil unrest triggered by the murder of George Floyd for changing the role of a City Council member for the worse.</p><p>“More time needs to be spent advocating for the people you were elected to represent, and less on resolutions speaking out on things that happened half-way around the world," O'Shea said. </p><p>“The majority of our children in public schools are reading below proficiency levels and their math scores are significantly below where they should be. We need to spend more time focusing on that and less on, `What’s the title we’re gonna give to the school. We’re gonna change the title.’ We’re gonna change the name on the bathroom door. But our children aren’t prepared to go out in the real world.”</p><p>O’Shea has been an outspoken advocate for the police officers and firefighters who live in his ward. He accused Johnson of using his first three budgets to shrink the Chicago Police Department by attrition. </p><p>“The police academy is empty right now. We’re gonna continue to see police districts across the city shrink in numbers,” he said. “When something happens in a neighborhood, you want to get more officers deployed to combat a crime pattern. That’s becoming less and less of an option.”</p><p>O’Shea was a leader of the renegade majority that rejected the mayor’s corporate head tax and muscled through an alternative city budget with major elements Johnson has either been unable to, or refused to, implement.</p><p>The mayor plans to renew his "tax the rich" mantra to help erase an <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/09/03/mayor-brandon-johnson-2027-budget-forecast-chicago-city-hall-deficit" >$882.4 million shortfall</a> in what could be his final budget. </p><p>But O’Shea said, "Before we start talking about revenue, taxes, property taxes, etc., we need to look within our government where can we make cuts. We need to put everything on the table. We have bloat in places. What departments can we make cuts at that don’t jeopardize public safety?”</p><p>Johnson has struggled to pass his last two budgets. He's issued three vetoes and been forced to accept a Zoning Committee chair he did not choose. His contentious relationship with the City Council continues to worsen. </p><p>O’Shea blamed an “unwillingness to come to the table to find compromise" and said "important people around" Johnson are "in over their heads.”</p><p>"Mayor of this city at this time would be difficult for anybody. But you can't succeed at it if you surround [yourself] with people who aren't going to give you good counsel," O'Shea said. </p>

Here’s how it went.</a></h3><p></p><h5>Reporting by <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydedujt-l-k/" target="_blank" >Somer Van Benton</a></h5><p><b>For Chicago's teens</b>: On Aug. 19, more than 160 teenagers were hanging out, eating food and taking photos at North Avenue Beach — a party just for the city's youth, thrown by nonprofit Project Exploration and the Mayor's Office of Education, Youth and Human Services. The mayor's office invested more than $10,000 for food, transportation, a video game truck, a handwashing station, a portable toilet, tables and chairs.</p><p><b>Key context</b>: Viral social media posts and news coverage showing large teen trends and "takeovers" have fueled debates about parent accountability ordinances, snap curfews, escort policies and other approaches to manage the gatherings. Project Exploration employs several teens who led the organizing of the Aug. 19 beach party while adults handled the logistics. City officials offered support, saying they want more safe spaces for teens to gather.</p><p><b>Adults dampen fun</b>: Youth organizers said it's a challenge to both create safe spaces and make teens feel welcome. Aug. 19's party was interrupted by adult volleyball players who refused to alter their plans for the city-sanctioned gathering, despite signs around the court and adult organizers and teens asking the volleyballers to wait until after the event ended. The players set up anyway, leaving some teens feeling discouraged and unwelcome in a public space they had gone through the proper channels to reserve.</p><p><b>Key quote</b>: "There were absolutely zero fights, there were zero weapons, there were zero altercations," said Janeicia Williams, who helped oversee the event. to meet for the first time, marking new era for local public transportation</a></h3><p></p><h5>Reporting by <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydedujt-l-n/" target="_blank" >David Struett</a></h5><p><b>NITA ride?</b> The Northern Illinois Transit Authority's board meets for the first time Thursday, officially launching the agency tasked with transforming Chicago-area public transit. NITA replaces the Regional Transportation Authority, which had governed CTA, Metra and Pace since 1974.</p><p><b>Key context</b>: The reshaping of public transit began last year when lawmakers passed the NITA bill, a last-minute, $1.5 billion bailout to save the agencies from service cuts. The NITA law also restructured transit governance, aiming to elevate CTA, Metra and Pace into world-class services — the NITA board has 20 directors appointed by the governor, mayor of Chicago, Cook County board president and the five collar counties.</p><p><b>What will it do?</b> NITA has several requirements and a timeline to complete them, including coordinating service — and unifying fares — between agencies, voting on whether to create a transit police department, deploying "transit ambassadors," mandating electric buses and more.</p><p><a class="Link" Conservatory fest embraces roots as celebration of ambient music, plant life</a></h3><p></p><h5>Reporting by <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydedujt-l-th/" target="_blank" >Selena Fragassi</a></h5><p>Plantasia is the one time every year when the greenhouse turns into a house party. Held at Garfield Park Conservatory on Thursday and Friday, it's a two-day celebration of ambient and electronic music set among palm trees and succulents that some believe is just as much for plants as it is for the people.</p><p>"I do believe plants have certain receptors to vibration," said performer Makaya McCraven, "and communication through vibration and connection is part of the intangibles of sound and music."</p><p>The local jazz luminary will headline the final day of Plantasia, which is now in its eighth year. But the roots of the event and this intersection between music and horticulture go back decades to Mort Garson's 1976 electronic album made for plants: "Mother Earth's Plantasia: Warm earth music for plants … and the people that love them."</p><p>While the first year of Plantasia was wholly devoted to recreating Garson’s soundscape, the program has since expanded to welcome ambient and experimental artists of all flavors performing original works.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydedujt-l-tk/" target="_blank" ><b>READ MORE</b></a></p><hr><p></p><h4>YOUR DAILY QUESTION ☕️</h4><p><b>What iconic Chicago building would you love to tour? entries.title: Chicago school board candidates sign pledge to ban AI use in schools
entries.summary: <p><i>This story was </i><a class="Link" href="https://www.chalkbeat.org/chicago/2026/09/01/chicago-school-board-candidates-pledge-three-year-ai-ban/" target="_blank" ><i><u>originally published</u></i></a><i> by Chalkbeat. Sign up for their newsletters at </i><a class="Link" href="https://ckbe.at/newsletters" target="_blank" ><i><u>ckbe.at/newsletters</u></i></a>.</p><p>Roughly half of the 45 candidates running for the Chicago school board have signed <a class="Link" href="https://assets.nationbuilder.com/ilfps/pages/2762/attachments/original/1785611686/Human-centered_Ed_Pledge_and_Explainer_July_2026.pdf?1785611686" target="_blank" ><u>a pledge to adopt a three-year ban on artificial intelligence</u></a> use by CPS students and educators.</p><p>Crafted by a local nonprofit, the pledge also calls for eliminating school screen time before third grade and limiting it in later grades. It demands that the district hire a chief privacy officer and ban the collection of student biometric data, such as voice recordings captured by literacy software.</p><p>“The risks of AI are absolutely outweighing the benefits right now,” said Cassie Creswell, the head of Illinois Families for Public Schools, a parent advocacy group that has lobbied for more student privacy protections. “It’s perfectly possible to have a low-tech education and learn everything you need to know.”</p><p>The nonprofit wanted to leverage the city’s first races to elect all 21 members of the school board to exact commitments from candidates, Creswell said, though last week she also called on the current, partly elected board to consider AI restrictions this fall. So far, <a class="Link" href="https://humancenteredcps.com/?link_id=2&can_id=5b0909209d625124a7ff92322070b0b2&source=email-statement-on-chicago-public-schools-canceling-plans-to-roll-out-google-gemini-for-students-continue-use-of-amira&email_referrer=email_3364915&email_subject=statement-cps-canceling-google-gemini-rollout-for-students-continuing-use-of-ai-literacy-product-amira&&" target="_blank" ><u>24 candidates have signed the pledge</u></a>.</p><p>The local push comes amid <a class="Link" href="https://www.chalkbeat.org/2026/03/17/jared-cooney-horvath-says-ed-tech-hurts-learning-a-look-at-the-evidence/" target="_blank" ><u>a national parent backlash against education technology</u></a>, including AI-powered software. But some Chicago school board candidates, district officials, and others said the pledge goes too far, denying educators useful tools and limiting their ability to help students thoughtfully and safely navigate an ubiquitous technology.</p><p>“I think an outright ban is unproductive, and it really negates our responsibility, which is to come up with better solutions so our kids can both access this stuff, but also so that we don’t do irreparable harm to them,” said Janice Jackson, a former CPS CEO who is now leads the Education and Society Program at the nonpartisan think tank the Aspen Institute.</p><p>In a statement, Chicago Public Schools said it remains “steadfast in its deliberate, responsible approach to artificial intelligence.” It noted that <a class="Link" href="https://www.chalkbeat.org/chicago/2026/07/10/illinois-teachers-get-guidance-on-how-to-use-ai-in-schools/" target="_blank" ><u>the Illinois State Board of Education’s recently released AI guidelines</u></a> for school districts references CPS’ AI guidebook as a model.</p><p>Creswell points to a recent move by CPS to shelve a plan to give high school students access to Gemini — Google’s AI chatbot — as an early win for the effort, though CPS officials said they only briefly weighed that plan and nixed it last spring.</p><p>The district said officials considered “an aspirational plan” to enable Gemini access on its high schoolers’ Google Classroom accounts after a small group of educators tested the tool without letting students access it. But the plan was put on hold last May based on input from teachers “to prioritize individual school readiness and educator training.”</p><p>“CPS embraces AI’s potential to enhance learning while remaining fully committed to safeguarding critical thinking and student data privacy,” the district’s statement said.</p><p>The district said a group of high school students spent the summer designing a new Student Voice AI Council and drafting a Student AI Playbook.</p><p>Board member Debby Pope, an appointee and retired educator running to represent district 2b, who signed the pledge, worries about AI’s potential to undermine students’ ability to think creatively, write, and ferret out misinformation.</p><p>“It’s extremely important to take an approach of caution and care so we raise a generation that has critical thinking abilities and understands the importance of using multiple sources of information,” she said.</p><p>But she said she is concerned that an outright ban might hamper the district’s ability to teach kids already widely using the technology how AI works and how to navigate its pitfalls.</p><p>Ellen Rosenfeld, who is running to represent district 4b unopposed, didn’t sign the pledge. She shares many of the concerns in the pledge and supports taking a more critical look at tech use in CPS.</p><p>“I am concerned that on AI, we are building the plane while we’re flying it,” she said.</p><p>But she said she was uncomfortable signing a sweeping document with a yearslong commitment. She said she is unsure how much jurisdiction the board has to impose such a policy.</p><p>Some momentum for technology restrictions is building nationally. Earlier this year, Illinois joined a majority of states in adopting <a class="Link" href="https://www.chalkbeat.org/chicago/2026/06/01/illinois-lawmakers-pass-cellphone-ban-in-school-classrooms/" target="_blank" ><u>a new law restricting student cell phone use in schools</u></a> that will go into effect next year.</p><p>But the state’s AI guidance is nonbinding, imposing no requirements on how districts regulate the technology’s use. Earlier this summer, the school board in Los Angeles — whose <a class="Link" href="https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-06-21/carvalho-resigns-as-lausd-superintendent-amid-federal-investigation" target="_blank" ><u>superintendent resigned amid a federal probe</u></a> into a costly failed AI chatbot contract — passed <a class="Link" href="https://www.npr.org/2026/08/11/nx-s1-5913745/screen-limits-begin-la-schools" target="_blank" ><u>a policy banning screen time before the second grade</u></a>. This week, New York City is releasing <a class="Link" href="https://www.chalkbeat.org/newyork/2026/09/02/nyc-schools-to-set-ai-policy-ban-screen-time-limits/" target="_blank" ><u>a new policy that would restrict student AI use</u></a> in the elementary and middle grades and set screen time limits though it stops short of a full moratorium.</p><p>Creswell, of Illinois Families for Public Schools, said the nonprofit’s Pledge to Protect Human-Centered Education was also inspired by <a class="Link" href="https://www.brookings.edu/articles/a-new-direction-for-students-in-an-ai-world-prosper-prepare-protect/" target="_blank" ><u>a recent Brookings report</u></a> suggesting that AI’s potential harms to students exceed the possible benefits. She said tech use in CPS and its cost to the district have expanded without enough evidence these tools are improving learning or vendors are safeguarding student privacy. The nonprofit is taking particular aim at Amira, an AI-powered tool for struggling readers that CPS says has shown promising results in supplementing more traditional instruction.</p><p>Jackson, the former CPS CEO, said school districts need to be more discerning in selecting education technology tools. A lot of them are “junk,” she said, and she does worry about how companies are collecting and using student data.</p><p>At the same time, she said teachers are embracing helpful AI-powered tools, for example using AI to more efficiently plan lessons geared to diverse student needs. Failing to teach smart, responsible use of a technology that has come to permeate daily life can leave students at a disadvantage compared with peers at better resourced districts.</p><p>“I don’t think we get rid of technology and educate a bunch of kids who don’t know how to use these tools efficiently, because that doesn’t set them up for success,” she said. “But I do think it’s a moment to take a step back and make sure there are guardrails in place.”</p><p><i>This story has been updated to include information on a newly released New York City policy on student use of AI.</i></p><p><i>Mila Koumpilova is Chalkbeat Chicago’s senior reporter covering Chicago Public Schools. Contact Mila at </i><a class="Link" href="mailto:mkoumpilova@chalkbeat.org" target="_blank" ><i><u>mkoumpilova@chalkbeat.org</u></i></a><i>.</i></p><p><i>Chalkbeat is a nonprofit news organization </i><a class="Link" href="https://www.chalkbeat.org/chicago/2026/09/01/chicago-school-board-candidates-pledge-three-year-ai-ban/" target="_blank" ><i><u>covering public education</u></i></a><i>.</i></p>

entries.title: Alcalde Johnson pierde aliado clave luego de que concejal Rodríguez no busca reelección
entries.summary: <p>El alcalde Brandon Johnson está perdiendo a uno de sus aliados más firmes en el Concejo Municipal.</p><p>El concejal Mike Rodríguez (22.º), presidente del Comité de Desarrollo Laboral y quien ayudó a Johnson a concretar dos de los logros de su agenda progresista de los que más se enorgullece, decidió no buscar la reelección.</p><p>“Mi hija entra a la secundaria. Tengo cuatro años más con esa hermosa bebé. Tengo un padre enfermo. Tengo un hijo campeón de ajedrez... Es el momento adecuado para mí”, para dar un paso atrás, dijo Rodríguez, quien prácticamente respaldó a la miembro del distrito policial 10, Elianne Bahena, como su sucesora.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-080000" name="module-080000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>“Estaba en un torneo de fútbol en Minnesota con mi hijo en julio… y recuerdo que tuve que alejarme de la multitud porque quería que los miembros del Concejo Municipal escucharan mi ‘sí’ en una reunión de comité. Durante la mitad del viaje, mi esposa les decía a mis hijos que se callaran porque yo tenía llamadas de trabajo... Quiero estar presente para mi familia”, agregó.</p><p>Rodríguez, de 48 años, es el segundo concejal veterano en elegir retirarse de la política en lugar de buscar la reelección. El concejal Marty Quinn (13.º), uno de los críticos más duros de Johnson, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/fran-spielman-show/2026/07/08/one-of-mayor-brandon-johnson-most-ardent-city-council-adversaries-wont-seek-reelection-in-2027" target="_blank" >también deja el Concejo Municipal</a>.</p><p>Respaldado por el congresista saliente Jesús “Chuy” García, Rodríguez pasó sus dos mandatos en el Concejo Municipal presentándose como un defensor de la clase trabajadora. Fue el principal copatrocinador de una Ordenanza de Semana Laboral Justa que impulsó protecciones clave para empleados con horarios impredecibles.</p><p>Impulsó otra protección importante para los trabajadores de Chicago con la Ordenanza de Licencia Pagada que otorgó a los empleados un mínimo de 10 días de descanso pagados. Para Rodríguez, esos logros fueron más personales que políticos.</p><p>La motivación se remonta a su infancia. Recordó que en vida, su madre pudo llevarlo a él, a su hermano y a su hermana al Taste of Chicago —junto con una pizza de Home Run Inn y un paseo en barco— porque ella era trabajadora sindicalizada que tenía tiempo libre pagado.</p><p>“Pienso en cuántos habitantes de Chicago ni siquiera pueden tomarse un día para quedarse con su hijo en casa si está enfermo y no pueden ayudar a una madre o un padre enfermo si necesitan estar ahí”, dijo Rodríguez al Chicago Sun-Times.</p><p>“Por eso me sentí tan orgulloso de ser el defensor y aprobar la política de licencia pagada más amplia del país. En los primeros dos años de esta administración, pondré mi historial como presidente del comité de desarrollo laboral contra el de cualquiera en la historia de la Ciudad”, afirmó.</p><p>Ambos logros de la lista progresista de Johnson se alcanzaron al inicio de la administración del alcalde. Pero desde entonces ha sido cuesta abajo.</p><p>Johnson usó su tercer veto para preservar otra promesa clave de su agenda progresista —eliminar el salario submínimo para trabajadores con propinas— y logró que se mantuviera.</p><p>Rodríguez reconoció que la “lucha por defender a la clase trabajadora” continúa y no se “resolverá en esta administración municipal ni en la siguiente”. Pero espera sumarse a su colega del suroeste, la concejal Julia Ramírez (12.º), para aprobar protecciones para trabajadores de almacenes antes de dejar el cargo en mayo.</p><p>El mandato de Rodríguez incluyó la fallida implosión de la chimenea de Hilco en la antigua fábrica de carbón Crawford y el Operativo Midway Blitz, que amenazó a los residentes de La Villita hace un año. En un momento, miembros del propio personal de Rodríguez fueron detenidos.</p><p>Rodríguez dijo que no olvidará estar en la calle 26 y Pulaski viendo al ex comandante Greg Bovino, de la Patrulla Fronteriza, y a sus agentes girar a la izquierda por la calle 26 y llevarse a un hombre frente a un niño de 6 años.</p><p>“Ese niño fue testigo de que se llevaron a una persona de forma indiscriminada porque tenía la piel morena. Lo que vi fue el demonio en Bovino. Lo miré a los ojos”, dijo Rodríguez.</p><p>“Me lanzan una bola de gas al pie. Ese humo llenó el auto del niño que estaba sentado ahí. Recuerdo ver a ese niño devastado, llorando, sin saber qué diablos estaba pasando. Solo pienso en que esto será un recuerdo inolvidable para ese niño por el resto de su vida”.</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (IA) y editado por los seres humanos de</i> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a></p>

entries.title: 2nd measles case confirmed in Kane County
entries.summary: <p>A second measles case has been confirmed in Kane County weeks after the area's first confirmed case, according to health officials. </p><p>The person was vaccinated against measles and in contact with the first case, which was <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/health/2026/08/25/measles-kane-county" target="_blank" >reported Aug. 24</a>, according to the Kane County Health Department. </p><p>While a vaccination protects against measles, breakthrough cases, where a vaccinated person can get measles, still occur, health officials said. People who are vaccinated and develop measles are generally less likely to experience severe illness or complications and may be less likely to transmit the virus.</p><p>The first confirmed case in Kane County included two possible exposure locations: <br></p><ul class="rte2-style-ul" id="rte-b87aa9e2-ad33-11f1-a7ca-15c2c640663f"><li>Kaneland High School in Maple Park on Aug. 18, during the school day. </li><li>Next Generation Pediatric Clinic in South Elgin on Aug, 21, between 12:30 p.m. and 4 p.m.</li></ul><p>As of Tuesday, there were 11 reported measles cases in the state, according to the Illinois Department of Public Health. <br></p>

entries.title: NITA elects its first leader as oversight agency for CTA, Metra, Pace
entries.summary: <p>The Northern Illinois Transit Authority, in its first public meeting, elected a chairman to lead the oversight agency tasked with rethinking Chicago-area public transit.</p><p>The NITA board voted unanimously Thursday to elect Tom Kotarac, a former Regional Transportation Authority director who had been leading a NITA transition committee.</p><p>The board was also expected to choose an executive director and use its new powers to expand a low-income reduced fare program to the CTA and make student passes work all-year-round.</p><p>NITA replaces the RTA in governing the CTA, Metra and Pace. Plans for the new agency began last year when lawmakers bailed out the transit agencies, but not before reforming how they operate. </p><p>NITA has been granted increased authority to set fares and coordinate service with $1.5 billion of extra yearly cash to make public transit safer and more reliable.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/transportation/2026/09/10/nita-northern-illinois-transit-authority-cta-metra-pace" target="_blank" >NITA, Chicago’s new transit agency, is meeting for the first time. What will it change?</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>The new NITA chairman emphasized the gravity of the task.</p><p>The "NITA Act has given us something that's really rare in government and in organizations. And it's a genuine opportunity for a fresh start," Kotarac said.</p><p>"If we succeed years from now, people will look back and say, 'This is more than just avoiding the 'fiscal cliff,'" Kotarac said. "We'll look back to when we chose to do something transformational."</p><p>The NITA law mandates several changes to public transit. The agency has been given increased power over CTA, Metra and Pace to make those decisions.</p><p>Next year, NITA will decide whether to create a new police department to patrol across all three transit agencies. NITA must also deploy trained "transit ambassadors" by next July, as the agency prioritizes addressing concerns about security.</p><p>NITA must also simplify tickets and transferring between agencies.</p><p>Under the NITA system, Kotarac said, "a customer can travel from Chicago to the suburbs — to Huntley, and even Rockford — with one easy-to-use system. One ticket, one timetable and one network, just as it says in the NITA Act."</p><p>A "unified" ticket system must be in place by February 2030, according to the law.</p>

entries.title: Bulls announce plans on how they will honor Stacey King this season
entries.summary: <p>The Bulls have used the last few months to figure out how they wanted to best remember broadcaster Stacey King after he died at the age of 59 back on June 7, and on Thursday they announced those plans.</p><p>Throughout the 2026-27 campaign, the team’s uniform will feature a band on the upper-left side with the name “King” and a microphone icon on it, honoring the two-plus decades he spent as the franchise’s broadcaster.</p><p>There will also be a Stacey King Celebration Night on Feb. 4, several days after what would have been King’s 60<sup>th</sup> birthday (Jan. 29). More information regarding the details of that evening – which is against the Oklahoma City Thunder – will be made available later.</p><p>King was not only a member of the first three NBA championship teams from 1991-93, but turned into the voice of the organization post-playing career, serving as an Emmy Award-winning broadcaster.</p><p>As far as a replacement, the Sun-Times reported the rotation of Kendall Gill, Will Perdue, Scott Williams and Robbie Hummel throughout this upcoming season.</p>

entries.title: QB Gavin Gardiner showcases improved game, helps St. Patrick start 3-0
entries.summary: <p>Gavin Gardiner looks like a different player.</p><p>Not only has the 6-6 senior quarterback elevated his skills from a year ago, but he’s starting to fill out his frame.</p><p>Up 30 pounds after his offseason training, Gardiner has unbeaten St. Patrick cooking on offense. The Shamrocks (3-0) are averaging 51.7 points per game.</p><p>“Our offensive coordinator, Byron Dawkins, he’s been awesome,” Gardiner said. “He’s really helped me, especially with my reads and footwork. It’s awesome to play in his offense. Our offensive line is protecting me and I haven’t been sacked yet this season. Our run game’s really clicking. Our receivers are getting in the right spots.”</p><p>Class 5A playoff qualifiers a year ago, the Shamrocks have blown out Rolling Meadows, St. Viator and Marian Catholic. He’s only made two starts, but Gardiner has 619 passing yards and eight touchdowns on a 65% completion rate. Even with Gardiner sitting out Week 3 due to rest, backup quarterback Kierre Wilson led St. Patrick to a 45-7 win.</p><p>“Byron’s helped me so much with my confidence and my footwork,” Gardiner said. “I’ve really progressed on the run and off platform. Last year, I was strictly a pocket guy. I never really got on the move. This year, I have a rushing touchdown and we have a lot of moves outside of the pocket. I really worked on that this offseason.”</p><p>Executing RPOs and showing improved mobility, Gardiner has spread the ball around. He connected with receiver A.J. Henning five times for 127 yards and two touchdowns during a 54-27 win over Rolling Meadows. The next week, Gardiner found Nicholas Miro six times for 120 yards and two touchdowns in a 56-14 thrashing of St. Viator.</p><p>“Our concepts are working really well with our run game and our play action game,” Gardiner said. “We have good run fakes up front and we’re putting linebackers in conflict. I’ve had a lot of passes over the middle through tight windows. Our receivers are making the right reads on some of our deeper concepts and we’re clicking right now.”</p><p>The Shamrocks have been as effective on the ground as they’ve been through the air. Running behind a tough offensive line that includes 6-8 Minnesota recruit Dylan Mota, senior back Jayden Miranda has 426 yards and seven touchdowns on almost 7 yards per carry. St. Patrick has more points than any CCL team through three weeks.</p><p>“Our RPO reliefs on these run plays just put the defense in so much stress,” Gardiner said. “They can’t be right and that’s kind of my job. Every run play, we have some sort of RPO tag for the most part, so we’re getting the right numbers in the box and our linemen are going to get the job done up front. ... Jayden, he’s running people over.”</p><p>Gardiner is one of only a few returning starting quarterbacks in the CCL. He took the reins his junior season, St. Patrick’s first under head coach Tom Zbikowski. Gardiner started 11 games and threw for 2,094 yards, 16 touchdowns and 11 interceptions as the Shamrocks advanced to the second round of the playoffs, losing to Cary-Grove.</p><p>St. Patrick faces Marmion this week and will have tough tests against Mount Carmel, Joliet Catholic and Nazareth as the year progresses. For Gardiner, whose goals include hitting 3,000 passing yards and a state championship, the focus remains week to week.</p><p>“We’re all confident in each other,” Gardiner said. “We’ve been doing it together since freshman year. We haven’t had many transfers and we’ve had a couple of additions to the receiver room. Our chemistry is very high.”</p><p>Zbikowski, a former Buffalo Grove and Notre Dame star who played in the NFL, spoke highly of his returning quarterback in the summer.</p><p>“Gavin looks as sharp as I’ve seen him look,” Zbikowski said. “Him arm strength is there and his decisions are there. He was always a good decision maker, but seeing the extra weight on him has been good. ... We’re all getting on the same page, but it’s good having a leader like Gavin who can pick it all up and translate it to all of the boys.”</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://www.shawlocal.com/friday-night-drive/" target="_blank" >Read more high school football coverage on Friday Night Drive.</a></p>

entries.title: Memories of 9/11 horror still fresh after a quarter-century
entries.summary: <p>On Sept. 11, 2001, my older son was 5, and some mornings played video games on my computer. So I wasn't plugged into the world that morning. I didn't know that American Airlines Flight 11 had struck the North Tower at 7:46 a.m. Chicago time. I did not own a cell phone.</p><p>At the Northbrook Metra station, stepping onto the 8:17 Downtown, I heard a woman down the platform say something about the World Trade Center being hit by a plane.</p><p>At Union Station, knots of people stood around, talking. I asked one: what kind of plane hit the Twin Towers?</p><p>"A 767," he said. That startled me. I had assumed it would be a Cessna.</p><p>"That's a big plane," I said, dully.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-cd0000" name="module-cd0000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Opinion bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Opinion</h2></div> </div><p>At Wacker Drive, people were pouring out of the Sears Tower, fanning out in all directions. I noticed that, as they hurried along, they looked up, scanning the sky. As if they expected to see a plane go into the building at any moment.</p><p>There was a Billy Goat Tavern on Washington, open for breakfast. I stepped inside. Everyone was just standing there in silence, watching the North Tower collapse on TV. I joined them. You could hear the eggs sizzling on the grill.</p><p>The paper was still at 401 N. Wabash. I was on the editorial board and walked into editorial page editor Steve Huntley's office.</p><p>"How do you spell 'Osama bin Laden?'" he asked. I'd never heard the name but went to my office to find out.</p><p>I used to say there were two shocks about Sept. 11 — the first was that it happened, that four planes were hijacked by 19 men wielding box cutters. Two crashed into New York's World Trade Center, toppling the towers. A third hit the Pentagon and a fourth crashed into a field in Shanksville, Pennsylvania, after passengers stormed the cockpit; 2,973 men, women and children died that day.</p><p>There was a time when I wouldn't feel obligated to spell out the details. But more than a third of Americans have no living memory of Sept. 11, 2001, and it would not be surprising if 9/11 is news to some — just another crumb of dusty history they didn't learn in school.</p><p>Leading to the second shock of 9/11: that it went away, or at least ebbed. Because for days and weeks and months, it seemed that 9/11 was a permanent condition, a radiating, bottomless shock, sorrow and stupefaction. But ebb it did, slowly receding, like a tide going out. And now 25 years have gone by, and attention must be paid again.</p><p>We put out "Extras" in those days — special editions to update breaking news stories, hawked at newsstands downtown. Our first was headlined "UNSPEAKABLE HORROR" — I remember looking at "Unspeakable" and thinking, "Really? 'Cause we're trying to flippin' speak it." The second was better: "TERROR!" </p><p>I filed an insert to our editorial, then asked the City Desk what I could do to help. Go into the Loop, see what's up. So I went back to the Sears Tower and interviewed disappointed tourists who had planned to visit the Sky Deck. At 111 W. Washington, I watched an employee, ex-Marine Johnny Washington, lower the building's flags to half-mast.</p><p>"This is terrible," he said. </p><p>Back at the newsroom, our publisher John Cruickshank, a smart and decent Canadian, made a little speech. This was the biggest story of our lives, yes, but it is also an enormous human tragedy. We should pray. So we all bowed our head and uttered a little silent prayer, then went back to work. I'm not generally a fan of public displays of piety, but it seemed the right thing to do, and I was grateful.</p><p>I won't attempt to summarize all the bad that came from those attacks. Two needless wars, in Afghanistan and Iraq. Over 7,000 U.S. military deaths — twice the loss of 9/11 — not to forget over 200,000 civilian deaths. I don't recall that being called a genocide. The sweeping, intrusive Patriot Act. George W. Bush tried not to demonize Muslims, but others were not so scrupulous — anti-Islamic hate was a major leg of Donald Trump's winning campaigns, and he barred immigration wholesale from Muslim countries. </p><p>On Sept. 12, 2001, I showed my older boy the front page of the New York Times, its photo of an explosion boiling out of the World Trade Center, and asked him what he thought about the picture, worried how he was processing 9/11's enormity. He said it looked beautiful — he thought it was a flower, a red rose, and I didn't correct him. The horror was very hard to wrap your mind around. It still is.</p>
entries.author: Neil Steinberg

entries.title: Chicago-area consultant, along with other experts, raised alarms about sloppy airport security before 9/11
entries.summary: <p>In the 25 years since the 9/11 terror attacks, there’s been considerable examination of how they could have been prevented.</p><p>What if our intelligence agencies had communicated with each other better? What if our foreign policy in the Middle East had been different? </p><p>What if warning signs were taken more seriously? What if the U.S. had succeeded in capturing or killing al-Qaeda leader Osama bin Laden in the 1990s?</p><p>Not to be overlooked: just how porous the front line security was at U.S. airports — along with weak security oversight by the federal government that allowed the airlines to handle screening with low-cost contractors and few prohibitions on what’s in purses, pockets and carry-ons.</p><p>After all, certain knives and blades were legally allowed on commercial aircraft at the time — and al-Qaeda terrorists took full advantage of that loophole by using box cutters to overtake the crew and passengers on flights they hijacked.</p><p>But had decision makers taken heed from a once-confidential security report by an Elmhurst consultant in the mid-1990s, as well as many other voices of concern and reform prior to 9/11, some experts wonder whether things could have ended differently.</p><p>The report — compiled by the Conley Group at the behest of officials at O’Hare Airport, which was and is overseen by City Hall — slammed aviation security practices before 9/11.</p><p>Obtained by the Chicago Sun-Times in 2002 and publicized then in a news story, the report advocated in the years leading up to the attacks for the public sector to assume screening for fliers and luggage, with O’Hare a proposed site to test the concept and expand from there.</p><p>At the time, airlines handled their screening duties by hiring private companies known for high employee turnover, lax training and cheap wages to staff the checkpoints. Critics said the aim was less about safety but rather to screen as swiftly and inexpensively as possible to enhance passenger convenience, and profits.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> class="Figure-credit"><p>Sun-Times archives.</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Mistakes, such as letting banned items through checkpoints, were relatively common, records show.</p><p>Not that there were many restrictions on carry-on items imposed back then by the Federal Aviation Administration, the public agency that regulates U.S. airports, airlines and airspace.</p><p>An airline industry trade group recommended that screeners confiscate pepper spray if detected, but the FAA did not technically bar it from commercial flights, according to published accounts. And some of the 9/11 hijackers apparently used a form of chemical agent during the attacks.</p><p>The FAA did ban blades over four inches, but that allowed smaller knives, razors and box cutters to be carried on, as hijackers did on 9/11 — though two aviation trade groups had advised that even smaller blades not be let through checkpoints, according to published accounts.</p><p>The Conley report suggested that by giving security duties to the Chicago Department of Aviation, the arm of City Hall that runs O’Hare and Midway airports, they’d be able to attract better workers and improve spotting dangerous items.</p><p>And if it worked out there, the concept could be exported to other airports, officials said at the time.</p><p>“I have to believe that the whole security environment would have been better” had the report’s conclusions been embraced earlier, Bob Monetti said in 2002. An aviation safety and security advocate, Monetti lost his son in the Pan Am 103 bombing over Lockerbie, Scotland, in 1988.</p><p>“Whether it would have stopped” 9/11 “or not, obviously you can't say,” Monetti said. “But the likelihood would have been people would be better trained, equipped and motivated.”</p><p>The FAA was aware of the report but it’s not clear why they didn’t allow such a test program at O’Hare. However, some worried it could lead to a lack of security “standardization” around the country, while others pointed to the influence of the airlines, who presumably would have had to plunk down more money to pay for any changes.</p><p>The Conley report said the O’Hare project would’ve likely cost about $3 million more annually.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Figure-credit"><p>AP</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>David Mosena, a former Chicago aviation commissioner, told the Sun-Times in 2002: "The FAA’s call was to leave it the way it was and not have different units of government or states or cities or even the feds be security screeners for airports, so it didn’t go anywhere. I think they were under some pressure from the airlines not to make dramatic changes in the system.”</p><p>It’s unclear if and how the Conley report focused on expanding prohibited carry-on items, but others in the aviation industry did raise concerns before 9/11 about non-prohibited objects that could be used for weapons.</p><p>Numerous studies also flagged flaws with the pre-9/11 security system at U.S. airports, including the U.S. General Accounting Office which noted days after 9/11: “As we reported in June 2000, tests of screeners revealed significant weaknesses as measured in their ability to detect threat objects located on passengers or contained in their carry-on luggage.”</p><p>“In 1987, screeners missed 20 percent of the potentially dangerous objects used by FAA in its tests. At that time, FAA characterized this level of performance as unsatisfactory. More recent results have shown that as testing gets more realistic — that is, as tests more closely approximate how a terrorist might attempt to penetrate a checkpoint — screeners’ performance declines significantly.”</p><p>The GAO also wrote that “of 102 other countries with international airports, 100 have placed screening responsibility with the airports or the government; only 2 other countries — Canada and Bermuda — place screening responsibility with air carriers” besides the U.S.</p><p>Former FAA administrator Jane Garvey recently recalled that there was a pending rule under review around the time the administrations changed, with President George W. Bush taking office in January 2001 as Bill Clinton left, that would’ve had the government assume airport security more directly.</p><p>“It’s often something I thought about, it was so close to the finish line,” Garvey said.</p><p>But she also wondered whether, had 9/11 not happened, “would the public at the time have accepted some of those rules that we now take for granted?”</p><p>“We had such a view of our own security and sense of freedom, I’m not quite sure.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a William Lipinski (D-Ill.)</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Sun-Times file</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Former U.S. Rep. William Lipinski (D-Ill.) was on the U.S. House’s aviation subcommittee and, with Midway in his district, one of Chicago’s aviation experts and advocates.</p><p>Long retired, Lipinski said recently that his panel held a hearing perhaps two years before 9/11 at which “many of the flaws that were unfortunately exploited on 9/11” were “pointed out.”</p><p>It was part of a larger effort to try to transfer security “responsibility from the airlines to the federal government,” he said.</p><p>While he and others “really saw the dangers” with the security system as it existed, the plans didn’t take flight.</p><p>After 9/11, the federal government did take over screening and security duties through the newly created Transportation Security Administration, or TSA, and vastly restricted what was allowed on airplanes, while enacting other measures including fortified cockpit doors and better explosive detection and passenger vetting.</p><p>The Conley report was eerily prophetic, stating: “The City has an opportunity to do a genuine good by taking the initiative and rectifying a serious problem. We feel that without this effort and commitment it is just a matter of time before these changes occur, borne of tragic necessity.”</p>

entries.title: Illinois officials put pressure on Trump administration to restore crisis lifeline for LGBTQ+ youth
entries.summary: <p>Illinois officials said it’s time to put pressure on the Trump administration to restore a lifeline they say can save the lives of LGBTQ+ youth experiencing mental health crises.</p><p>Officials, including U.S. Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi, are pushing the administration to restore the “Press 3” option on the nation’s 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, which previously provided specialized crisis services for LGBTQ+ youth.</p><p>“These were people, perhaps on the worst days of their life, at the worst hour of their day, reaching out for someone in the darkness to help save their life,” Krishnamoorthi said at a news conference Thursday.</p><p>The 988 Lifeline, including services for veterans and LGBTQ+ youth, was signed into law by President Trump during his first term. But in July 2025, the administration <a class="Link" href="https://www.samhsa.gov/about/news-announcements/statements/2025/samhsa-statement-988-press-3-option" target="_blank" >ended the specialized services</a> for LGBTQ+ youth, saying the Lifeline would no longer “silo” those services and would instead focus on “serving <i>all</i> help seekers.”</p><p>Krishnamoorthi said the service was canceled as part of the administration’s “anti-DEI efforts.” The administration, however, said the “Press 3” option had exhausted the funds allocated for 988 Lifeline LGBTQ+ subnetwork services.</p><p>The administration said Congress had allocated more than $33 million for the LGBTQ+ services in 2025, but the funding was fully spent by June.</p><p>But Illinois officials said LGBTQ+ youth face a higher risk of mental health crises and should have access to specialized crisis services that provide “affirming support.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div and other officials introduced the “<a class="Link" href="https://www.congress.gov/bill/119th-congress/house-bill/5434/text" target="_blank" >988 LGBTQ+ Youth Access Act of 2025</a>” in September 2025, seeking to pressure the federal government to restore the specialized services.</p><p>Krishnamoorthi said that despite bipartisan support and $33.1 million in available funding, the administration has refused to restore the services.</p><p>Dulce Quintero, secretary of the Illinois Department of Human Services, said the state had to “fill the gap” in services left by the federal government.</p><p>Quintero said the state began training all 988 Lifeline counselors in Illinois on LGBTQIA+ cultural competency. In the past year, Illinois received nearly 173,000 calls and was able to resolve 98% of them without further intervention, according to Quintero.</p><p>But while Illinois has been able to continue offering specialized services, she said that isn’t the case in other states.</p><p>“In Illinois we have an administration that supports this,” said Quintero. “That is not the reality in other states. We have been able to do this here in Illinois, but we need to make sure that it's available across and throughout the country. “</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div entries.title: Previewing Week 4's top high school football games
entries.summary: <p>It’s a loaded weekend around the area in Week 4. Here are previews of a few of the best games.</p><h3>No. 6 Brother Rice at No. 1 Loyola 7 p.m. Friday</h3><p>Brother Rice (2-1, 0-0 Catholic League Blue) has used a quarterback platoon of senior Rocco Galasso (193 passing yards) and freshman Sam Holcomb (437 total yards, nine total TDs). The Crusaders also have a pair of productive running backs in Army commit Jameson Davis and sophomore Aydan Yarbrough. On the other side of the ball, Notre Dame commit Brayden Parks and five-star junior Kameron McGee are one of the state's elite defensive line duos. Loyola (3-0, 0-0) also has a high-powered offense led by three juniors: quarterback Matthew Lee, running back Melo Maldonado and tight end Jordan McKinley. The Ramblers' defense has two shutouts, vs. Warren and St. Rita.</p><h3>No. 4 Oswego at No. 25 Bolingbrook, 7 p.m. Friday</h3><p>This might be the de facto Southwest Prairie West championship game. Returning Class 8A runner-up Oswego (3-0, 1-0) can move the ball effectively on the ground with junior Ammar Banire, who has offers from Indiana, Illinois and Iowa among others. Senior quarterback Drew Kleinhans gives the usually run-oriented Panthers another dimension, having passed for 560 yards and six touchdowns. Bolingbrook's Dareion Prescott, a 6-4, 255-pound edge, is a five-star prospect, the consensus No. 1 junior in Illinois and a top-20 player nationally. On offense, the Raiders (2-1, 1-0) lean on Oklahoma State-bound running back TJ Lewis.</p><h3>No. 9 Sandburg at No. 22 Homewood-Flossmoor, 7:30 p.m. Friday</h3><p>Sandburg (3-0, 0-0 SouthWest Suburban) has one of the season's notable victories, 35-28 to snap Montini's 25-game winning streak. Keep an eye on Eagles junior running back/defensive back Vinny Annel, who returned a kickoff for a TD, ran for 60 yards and had 10 tackles in last week's 37-14 win against Thornwood. Other impact players include quarterback Sean Ruisz, running back Quinn Durkin (Army) and tight end/receiver Lucas Matykiewicz (Northern Illinois). H-F (2-1, 0-1) opened with dominant shutouts of Bolingbrook and Richards before losing 38-7 to Lincoln-Way East last week. Wisconsin commit David Hill, a 6-3, 300-pound lineman, anchors the Vikings defense.</p><h3>No. 15 Glenbard West at No. 17 Downers Grove North, 7:30 p.m. Friday:</h3><p>Glenbard West (2-1, 1-0 West Suburban Silver) is historically one of the more run-heavy offenses in the area. But quarterback AJ Rayford and Northwestern-bound tight end Brady Johnson give the Hilltoppers a potent passing game this season. Another Northwestern commit, 6-8, 300-pound Josiah Wallace, anchors the offensive line. Junior Grant Georgas has 411 all-purpose yards and five touchdowns for Downers North (3-0, 1-0), including 113 yards and three scores in last week's shutout of Hinsdale Central.</p><h3>No. 12 Montini at No. 21 Nazareth, 7:30 p.m. Friday</h3><p>After piling up almost 4,300 total yards and 50 touchdowns for the Class 4A champs last season, senior quarterback Israel Abrams (Miami) is putting up big numbers again for Montini (2-1, 0-0 Catholic League Green). He has 675 yards and eight TDs passing along with three rushing scores as the Broncos are averaging 37 points a game. Nazareth (1-2, 0-0) has a typically challenging schedule with losses to IC Catholic and Mount Carmel sandwiched around a win against York.</p>

entries.title: Teen girl charged after shooting that critically wounded another girl during summer gathering
entries.summary: <p>A 17-year-old girl was charged in connection with a shooting that left another girl critically wounded earlier this summer during a rowdy gathering in West Garfield Park. </p><p>The girl, who was not named because she's underage, was arrested Wednesday in the Pullman neighborhood and charged with attempted first-degree murder, Chicago police said in a statement. </p><p>She allegedly shot another 17-year-old girl in her chest on July 5 during a large gathering in the 3800 block of West Maypole Avenue. She was taken to Stroger Hospital in critical condition. </p><p>About nine minutes later, at least six people were also shot on the same block. They were all in good condition at Stroger and Mount Sinai Hospital: two 17-year-old boys, an 18-year-old woman and man, a 19-year-old man and a 20-year-old man.</p><p>The girl was not charged for the other shooting. </p><p>After the shootings, a longtime resident on the block <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/07/05/7-shot-west-garfield-park" target="_blank" >described the gathering to the Sun-Times</a> as "total chaos." </p>
entries.author: Sun-Times Wire

entries.title: After Brewers sweep, Cubs fighting for playoff spot as wild-card standings tighten, series losses keep coming
entries.summary: <p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a>’ playoff fate is suddenly a lot more uncertain.</p><p>That’s what happens when you start the regular season’s home stretch winning just two of eight series.</p><p>This week’s three-game sweep at the hands of the rival Brewers <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/09/09/cubs-kevin-gausman-trade-deadline-jed-hoyer-brewers-starting-rotation-playoff-starter-clay-holmes-ian-happ-phil-maton" >all but put the NL Central race on ice</a>, putting the Cubs back by double digits in the standings with only 15 games remaining on their schedule.</p><p>Whether there will be any games past that, somewhat shockingly, remains to be seen.</p><p>But that’s how things are going for the Cubs, who have slipped from their perch controlling the NL wild-card race to second place behind the Phillies, with only a meager lead on the third-place Padres and next-in-line Diamondbacks, the latter another team that dealt them a recent series loss at the worst possible time.</p><p>Rather than spending the regular season’s final weeks tuning up for a planned run deep into October, the Cubs will need to fight to secure their ticket to the postseason, with three games apiece against the Pirates, Braves, Reds, Marlins and Red Sox. Two of those squads — the Braves and Red Sox — also have playoff seeding to fight for.</p><p>“We don’t have time to sulk,” righty pitcher Kevin Gausman said after Wednesday’s game, the team’s fourth straight loss. “We’ve just got to keep staying confident in this group.”</p><p>How did this happen?</p><p>The Cubs, after all, woke up Thursday still in statistical possession of baseball’s best offense, leading the sport with 774 runs scored, and far and away baseball’s best defense, leading the way with 107 defensive runs saved.</p><p>But a roller-coaster season has taken another dip, not exactly the same as when the bats went cold in late May and early June, though potentially just as costly.</p><p>On Aug. 12, the Cubs owned a 6½-game lead on the second-place Padres in the wild-card standings, further ahead of the D-backs and Phillies, who were tied for third. Since, they’ve gone 10-16, tumbling into their current predicament.</p><p>During this latest downturn, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/09/09/cubs-bullpen-closer-jacob-webb-daniel-palencia-trent-thornton-aaron-civale-shelby-miller-edward-cabrera-craig-counsell" >the Cubs’ bullpen has been a flashpoint</a>, headlined by closer Jacob Webb coughing up a trio of game-changing homers in recent weeks. But the starting rotation, too, has been plagued by inconsistency, with <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/09/01/cubs-home-runs-record-jed-hoyer-front-office-pitching-starting-rotation-playoffs-postseason-shota-imanaga-matthew-boyd" >team president Jed Hoyer’s worst fears</a> about a staff that could sink his team’s chances seemingly coming true.</p><p>That trade-deadline acquisitions Gausman and Clay Holmes have been among the offenders is troubling. Just a week ago, Hoyer described the two righties as “stabilizing forces,” and that’s what they were brought in to be. Then Holmes had perhaps the worst start of his career last weekend against the Marlins, while Gausman continued to swing back and forth between gems and clunkers, giving up three homers Wednesday in Milwaukee.</p><p>This week’s series in Wisconsin not just reinforced that the Cubs are a clear No. 2 in their rivalry with the best-in-baseball Brewers but saw them struggling to do even the things that made them contenders in the first place. They scored only four of their 12 runs in the series before the ninth inning and made a pair of rare defensive mistakes that led to runs in Wednesday’s loss.</p><p>“We’ve got to play good baseball,” manager Craig Counsell said. “We’re not playing good enough. There’s enough things we’re not doing in all areas.</p><p>“We’ve got to do a little bit more, collectively, to win games.”</p><p>That Brewers-shaped hurdle figures to be waiting for the Cubs at some point, should they advance in the postseason with a chance at revenge for last year’s ouster.</p><p>How would they clear it? A question without an answer after a rough three days and another season looking up at their rivals.</p><p>“The last two years, we’ve been chasing them,” left fielder Ian Happ said. “They have the best record in baseball now. They had the best record in baseball last year. They’ve done their job, and so you have to give them credit for that, all the way around as an organization.”</p><p>But right now, there are bigger fish to fry, chiefly ensuring they get into the postseason at all.</p><p>“Obviously, not the series we wanted to have here,” Happ said. “But we’ve put ourselves in a position where we control our own destiny, right?</p><p>“Our goal is to play playoff baseball, no matter how that shakes out, and give ourselves an opportunity. We have a little over two weeks to make that push and finish strong.”</p><p>The Cubs’ goals have been bigger than just reaching October, hungry for a World Series, a hunger <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/07/25/cubs-playoffs-brewers-pirates-nl-central-matthew-boyd-starting-rotation" >fueled by that playoff exit a year ago</a>.</p><p>But at this exact moment, the idea of the Cubs making it through the postseason gauntlet with all that troubles them, particularly on the pitching side, seems less realistic than it did not long ago.</p><p>Stellar play — and another climb on this season’s roller coaster — is not at all out of the realm of possibility, though, and the Cubs could find a discussion about them sputtering at the wrong time turning into one about them surging at the right time with a couple winning weeks.</p><p>The best offense? The best defense? The MVP favorite in Pete Crow-Armstrong? A hot-hitting free-agent splash in Alex Bregman? The big-money manager in Counsell? The fruits of an aggressive trade deadline?</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/09/01/cubs-kevin-gausman-cinnamon-rolls-world-series-blue-jays-dodgers-dansby-swanson-injury-justin-steele-iowa" >Championship ingredients</a>, without a doubt.</p><p>But will they get the chance to play for that championship?</p><p>Only if the next two weeks look a lot better than the last several.</p>
entries.author: Vinnie Duber

entries.title: Bears report: WR Rome Odunze limited again in practice
entries.summary: <p>Breaking down the Bears' Thursday practice at Halas Hall:</p><h3>Rome limited</h3><p>Wide receiver Rome Odunze, who hurt his calf a week ago, had limited participation. He was limited in the Bears' estimated practice report Wednesday. The Bears had Wednesday off.</p><p>If he can't play Sunday, Bears offensive coordinator Press Taylor said the Bears would be prepared.</p><p>"That's something we'll just let the medical staff tell us what his availability is and we'll roll from there," he said.</p><h3>Vet days</h3><p>Left guard Joe Thuney and defensive tackle Grady Jarrett each received a veteran day off on Thursday, a day where the Bears focused on special teams. The two captains are expected to practice Friday.</p><h3>Bagent still out</h3><p>Backup quarterback Tyson Bagent remained out with a back injury. He practiced Monday and Tuesday before going on the projected injury report Wednesday. If he can't dress for Sunday's game, 38-year-old Case Keenum would serve as the team's second-string quarterback.<br></p>

entries.title: Bears season predictions: Where will they finish in 2026?
entries.summary: <p>The Sun-Times' experts make their picks for the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears’</a> 2026 record:</p><h3>Patrick Finley</h3><p><b>10-7: </b>I believe this year's team is better than last season's. I also believe it's ridiculous to presume the Bears' takeaway, turnover and late-game good fortune can possibly continue at last year's pace — particularly against a first-place schedule.</p><h3>Jason Lieser</h3><p><b>11-6:</b> A lot has to go right merely for the Bears to match how they finished last season. The most important factor is whether Ben Johnson can help problem-solve on defense as well as he has on offense.</p><h3>Scoop Jackson</h3><p><b>10-6-1: </b>The 14 teams above the Bears in the NFL’s Football Power Index indicates that (especially with the Lions and Packers ahead of them) they might not know what we know. Or is it what we believe? Or what we hope?</p><h3>Steve Greenberg</h3><p><b>10-7: </b>There's this thing in football called defense, and — at the risk of sounding like a dinosaur — it's still kind of important. You say you've got a pretty good feeling about this Monsters "D"? Yeah, well, that makes one of us. I'm going with 10, but it's closer to a nine than it is to an 11. </p><h3>Jeff Agrest</h3><p><b>9-8:</b> Remember all those “nail-nibblers” last season, as Jeff Joniak calls them, that went the Bears’ way? The football gods do, and they’ll make sure a lot of breaks don’t go the Bears’ way.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/09/10/bears-panthers-week-1-predictions-picks-season-opener-charlotte-nc-odds-point-spread-caleb-williams-ben-johnson" >Bears predictions: Week 1 at Panthers</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Bears predictions: Week 1 at Panthers
entries.summary: <p>The Sun-Times’ <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> experts make their picks for the season opener in Charlotte, North Carolina:</p><h3>Patrick Finley</h3><p><b>Panthers, 27-26: </b>Winning on the road is hard. Particularly when the forecast at Bank of America Stadium on Sunday is for 89 degrees — and a 101-degree real feel. The Bears defense will have too much trouble with an offense the kids call "mid." <b>Last season</b>: 10-9.</p><h3>Jason Lieser</h3><p><b>Bears, 30-24:</b> The Bears can’t start slowly in any regard this season. They’re on the road, sure, but the Panthers were 8-9 last season, and even with some defensive concerns, the Bears should be able to handle them. <b>Last season:</b> 11-8.</p><h3>Scoop Jackson</h3><p><b>Panthers, 23-20: </b>Despite personal belief (and what’s written in a column) this Week 1 might mean more to Carolina than the Bears. The Panthers' new revamped defense will take the Bears offense by surprise. An early wake-up call. <b>Last season: </b>10-9.</p><h3>Steve Greenberg</h3><p><b>Bears, 30-27: </b>The Bears flip the script from last season by starting fast, building a nice lead and then hanging on for dear life. What, you thought this was going to be easy? Never. <b>Last season</b>: 13-6.</p><h3>Jeff Agrest</h3><p><b>Panthers, 27-23:</b> I believe in ghosts more than I believe in the Bears’ defense, which could be scary bad (see what I did there?). That’s why I’m taking the home underdog. Plus, Panthers quarterback Bryce Young’s ascent will continue. <b>Last season:</b> N/A.</p><p></p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/09/10/bears-season-predictions-final-record-2026-ben-johnson-caleb-williams-nfl" >Bears season predictions: Where will they finish in 2026?</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: DuSable Lake Shore Drive Bridge closing overnight for maintenance a week after getting stuck
entries.summary: <p>The DuSable Lake Shore Drive Bridge will be closed for overnight maintenance a week after the bridge spent over four hours stuck during a routine lift in extreme heat last week. </p><p>The closures are expected from 10 p.m. Thursday to 5 a.m. Friday and Tuesday from 10 p.m. to 5 a.m. Wednesday, according to the Chicago Department of Transportation. </p><p>The closures are in place in order for crews to conduct work in preparation for the fall boat run season, which includes maintenance "intended to help reduce the likelihood of the issue experienced last week," the department said. </p><p>On Sept. 2, the bridge was <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/transportation/2026/09/04/why-chicago-bridges-get-stuck-heat" target="_blank" >stuck for more than four hours</a> after a routine lift around 10 a.m. to let a yacht pass. </p><p>Crews spent hours trying to close the bridge completely. A Chicago Fire Department boat sprayed water to cool it down on Wednesday, which was Chicago’s second day <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/09/01/september-october-chicago-heat-wave-is-this-normal" target="_blank" ><u>under a heat advisory</u></a>.</p>
entries.author: Sun-Times Wire

entries.title: Des Plaines police said cop body camera wasn't on when 21-year-old with hedge trimmer was shot
entries.summary: <p>Des Plaines police said an officer didn’t activate his body camera before <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/09/09/des-plaines-police-officer-shoots-man-while-responding-to-domestic-disturbance" target="_blank" ><u>shooting</u></a> a 21-year-old with a hedge trimmer on his front lawn during an encounter.</p><p>Police on Wednesday were responding to a home in the 2000 block of Touhy Avenue at 2:32 p.m. for someone being “violent” and breaking windows when they found Ayham Babidi in the front yard with an electric hedge trimmer.</p><p>According to police, Babidi followed the officer, ignoring commands to drop the tool before the officer fired three shots. </p><p>Babidi was then taken to a local hospital where he later died, according to police.</p><p>Des Plaines police explained the officer didn’t have time to turn on his body camera “due to the rapid escalation of the incident.” </p><p>Officer dashcam and residential video footage from nearby homes that captured the shooting will be released “as soon as it no longer compromises the active investigation,” police said.<br></p>

entries.title: Sky’s Natasha Cloud knows what she wants in the next WNBA commissioner
entries.summary: <p>Reactions to commissioner <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky/2026/09/04/wnba-commissioner-cathy-engelbert-will-retire-in-december" >Cathy Engelbert’s retirement announcement </a>have ranged from cheers to takedowns to timid defenses.</p><p>But if there’s one thing everyone can all agree on, it’s that she had a tough job.</p><p>As WNBA commissioner, you don’t have the same luxuries as commissioners of the major men’s leagues.</p><p>You’re not <i>really</i> in charge, given that NBA commissioner Adam Silver is still your boss.</p><p>You can’t coast on a long track record of profitability like the NBA or NFL; the WNBA is only beginning to gain mainstream acceptance.</p><p>And you can’t block out the chaos stirred up by those who <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky/2026/08/24/enes-kanter-freedom-brought-middle-school-energy-to-the-wnba" >apparently can’t handle its success.</a></p><p>Crypto groups throwing sex toys onto the court. Former NBA players claiming to be women and declaring for the draft. Death threats and racialized abuse directed at players. Society keeps finding new and old ways to demean the league, even as its popularity grows.</p><p>Now it’s time to find out who’s crazy enough to take the job.</p><p>ESPN reported the first short list of commissioner candidates over the weekend. It included former players such as Swin Cash and Nneka Ogwumike, team presidents such as the Valkyries’ Jess Smith and the Liberty’s Keia Clarke, and league insiders such as Bethany Donaphin and Mark Tatum.</p><p>No surprise here: <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky" target="_blank" >Sky</a> veteran Natasha Cloud already has a strong opinion on who should fill the role.</p><p>“I hope it’s another player,” Cloud told the Sun-Times on Wednesday. “Whether it’s Swin, Nneka, even Keia. We don’t need a man in that position.</p><p>“I love Mark Tatum and what he’s been able to do in the NBA, but when it comes to our league and being understood as women, especially as a majority-minority league, I hope that we entrust in a player that understands what it means to be in this league.”</p><p>But wait, there’s more.</p><p>“I would obviously like a minority woman,” Cloud said. “I think being understood in these spaces of being protected from racism, transphobia, homophobia, you need a minority figure in that position that understands what it means to be 'other,' because we have not been protected.</p><p>“Cathy didn’t want to handle any of the extra [bleep] that’s going on outside of the court, so she’s washing her hands of it. But that’s not the best thing for our league.</p><p>“So in that next commissioner, there needs to be someone that takes priority in protecting us first and foremost and not allowing this league to be used as a pawn.”</p><p>Cloud said she tried to schedule a meeting with Engelbert after her altercation with former NBA player Enes Kanter Freedom, but the request was declined.</p><p>For Cloud, a more open line of communication with players is a must.</p><p>She also acknowledged that the commissioner ultimately reports to the owners and the NBA, and that a central part of the job is growing the league.</p><p>On that front, the players and the league might not be that far apart. Cloud and teammate Elizabeth Williams talked about globalizing the game, both by bringing the WNBA to other countries and ensuring international players can play in the W. Expanding the league’s global footprint was also a recurring theme in Engelbert’s final addresses.</p><p>Cloud and Williams called for more investment and transparency in officiating, too, some of which already appears to be in motion. The league will begin using a replay center next season, a significant investment intended to make reviews more streamlined and objective.</p><p>So that’s the good news for the future commissioner: The growth playbook includes some straightforward steps that other leagues have taken and the players support.</p><p>If only the rest of the job were that easy.</p><p>If the last few years have taught us anything, it’s that even Cloud’s perfect candidate will get tripped up along the way.</p>

entries.title: Team USA's Angel Reese and Caitlin Clark are enjoying time as teammates
entries.summary: <p>BERLIN — Angel Reese and Caitlin Clark's interactions are a subplot of the women's FIBA World Cup, the WNBA season and if you spend enough time on social media, a divided country. Clark and Reese have shown their relationship on the court is thriving.</p><p>Both players are intense and animated competitors, and their fanbases' are fiercely loyal. On much of social media you're either for Reese or for Clark. It has that feel of rooting for Duke or Carolina; Yankees or Red Sox or Bird or Magic.</p><p>The pair have definitely bonded so far in the World Cup in their national team debuts. Clark said many of the stories about their relationship are "false takes," saying she loves the fiery competitiveness that she and Reese share.</p><p>"No matter what, there's always going to be people that create those narratives and say whatever they want to say," Clark said. "There's definitely no stopping that and they're always going to be there. I think for ourselves, like I said, it's easy for us to just come in here and compete."</p><p>Reese has enjoyed playing with Clark as well as the other young members of the roster, including Paige Bueckers and Aliyah Boston.</p><p>"We know each other's game like the back of each other's hand, she knows my spots," Reese said of Clark. "We just continue to build chemistry because we know we're going to be USA teammates for a while."</p><p>In Thursday's quarterfinal that the U.S. won 108-56, the growing chemistry showed. The pair had a nifty pick-and-roll to end the first quarter that ended with a layup by Reese. The Atlanta Dream forward returned the favor hitting Clark on a fast break for an easy lay-in later in the game.</p><p>"She's got it for me a lot of times so it's probably finally due for me to get one to her and she easily finished it," Reese said smiling.</p><p>Clark and Reese have played together on the 2024 WNBA All-Star team that beat the U.S. Olympic team, but they will forever be joined at hips after their clash in the 2023 NCAA title game catapulted them into the center of debates.</p><p>Reese's LSU squad topped Clark's Iowa team in the matchup, but the players actions and interactions (who can forget Reese pointing to her ring finger in the closing seconds), drew attention to them.</p><p>Clark said she appreciates Reese's desire to win and her relentlessness on the court, saying "it's been fun to to be able to play with her."</p><p>Clark laughed recalling one incident in the tournament between she and Reese that has gotten some attention. When Clark was subbing in during the opener against China and started to step on the court before being officially told to, Reese, who was entering the game at the same time, pulled her back off the court.</p><p>"Well, the ref had gotten mad at me a couple of times prior, so she was saving me from the ref getting mad at me again," Clark said laughing.</p><p>In another fun moment, Reese was talking to the media after the tight win over Italy and Clark ducked past her, apologizing for interrupting her interviews. Reese smiled and gave Clark a high-five as she went by.</p><p>They'll be back on opposite sides soon enough — Reese's Atlanta Dream and Clark's Indiana Fever are both headed for the WNBA playoffs and both have 26-14 records. They could meet in the first round if the current seeds hold.</p><p>But for now, they share a common goal and the fact that Reese and Clark say they are having fun on the court together is good news for U.S. women's basketball fans. The duo could be part of a core group of players expected to be teammates in the next several Olympics.<br></p>

entries.title: West Loop tower that will bring neighborhood's first Aldi breaks ground
entries.summary: <p>The West Loop is a step closer to getting its first Aldi, as the formerly industrial neighborhood continues to grow its population.</p><p>Chicago-based Mavrek Development was joined by project partners Wednesday to break ground on Julep West Loop, a 25-story high-rise at 1000 W. Jackson Blvd. that will be anchored by a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2024/10/25/aldi-open-first-west-loop-store-amid-large-scale-expansion-plans" >22,000-square-foot Aldi</a>. The project includes land at 1000-24 W. Jackson Blvd., 230-38 S. Morgan and 1015-27 W. Adams streets.</p><p>Julep has been more than four years in the making, according to Mavrek. The Chicago Plan Commission <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2024/07/18/west-loop-apartment-projects-grocery-stores-chicago-plan-commission" >approved</a> the development
